====================================================================================================
2608.20961v1 | 2026-08-21 | updated 2026-08-21
TITLE: TreeWY: Speculative Verification for Gated DeltaNet Hybrids
AUTH: Sneha Murthy Ghantasala
COMMENT: 10 pages, 3 figures
ABS: Modern open models are hybrids: most layers are linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet, GDN) layers carrying a small fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value (KV) cache. This makes ordinary decoding memory-efficient, but hurts speculative decoding. To verify a batch of draft tokens and then roll back the rejected ones, today's systems snapshot the full recurrent state at every draft position for GDN layers, and those snapshots cannot be shared across branches of a draft tree, so a wide, high-acceptance tree becomes memory-infeasible. We remove the snapshots. Using a tree-structured WY transform of the gated delta rule, we compute every draft node's output with a single triangular solve and reconstruct only the one accepted state on commit, storing a small pseudo-value matrix instead of per-node states; the derivation depends only on the gated delta rule, not on any other architectural detail. In serving benchmarks on two scales of one hybrid model family (Qwen3.5 35B and 397B) this cuts speculative recurrent-state memory and KV-cache pressure at identical acceptance length, turning the freed HBM into higher throughput and much lower time-to-first-token (TTFT) wherever memory binds, and costing a few percent where it does not. For tree width the same memory buys affordability: a wider, higher-acceptance draft becomes possible, though not yet a throughput win.
====================================================================================================
2608.01651v1 | 2026-08-03 | updated 2026-08-03
TITLE: Bole: Efficient Tree Speculation for Hybrid-Attention Language Models
AUTH: Li Wang, Yi Su, Xiabao Wu, Chiran You, Yongchao Liu, Zhan Qiu, Juelu Zhang, Jiajun Zheng ...
COMMENT: 14 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables
ABS: Hybrid-attention large language models combine full attention with recurrent linear attention to reduce long-context inference costs, yet their autoregressive decoding remains memory-bound. Tree speculative decoding offers an attractive acceleration path, but existing tree-speculation systems are designed around the key--value caches of full-attention models. On hybrid models, they traverse recurrent layers branch by branch and materialize a full state for every proposal node, causing verification latency and transient memory to scale poorly with tree and batch sizes. We present Bole, a kernel--runtime co-design that enables efficient tree speculation for hybrid-attention LLMs. Bole transforms the linear-attention recurrence into a tree-structured closed form and realizes it with a resource-efficient GPU kernel, verifying all proposal nodes in parallel and accelerating linear-attention tree verification by 3.4--7.7$\times$. It losslessly encodes speculative state updates as token-level factors and reconstructs only the state selected after sampling, reducing transient state memory by 82--99$\times$ and freeing GPU capacity for KV caches. Its integration into SGLang, a widely deployed production LLM serving engine, couples efficient state management with a batch-wide verification budget calibrated to the complete hybrid forward. Across four models, two GPU platforms, and diverse datasets, Bole delivers up to $4.72\times$ the offline decode throughput of autoregressive decoding and up to $2.03\times$ that of the strongest tree-speculative baseline. Under online agent workloads, it reduces TTFT and TPOT by up to $67.6%$ and $49.9%$, respectively, over the strongest tree-speculative baseline.
====================================================================================================
2605.01106v1 | 2026-05-01 | updated 2026-05-01
TITLE: Component-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding in Hybrid Language Models
AUTH: Hector Borobia, Elies Seguí-Mas, Guillermina Tormo-Carbó
COMMENT: 29 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables. Code: https://github.com/hecboar/hybrid-speculative-decoding
ABS: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by drafting candidate tokens with a fast model and verifying them in parallel with the target. Self-speculative methods avoid the need for an external drafter but have been studied exclusively in homogeneous Transformer architectures. We introduce component-aware self-speculative decoding, the first method to exploit the internal architectural heterogeneity of hybrid language models, isolating the SSM/linear-attention subgraph as a zero-cost internal draft. We evaluate this on two architecturally distinct hybrid families: Falcon-H1 (parallel: Mamba-2 + attention per layer) and Qwen3.5 (sequential: interleaved linear and attention layers), with a pure Transformer control (Qwen2.5). Parallel hybrids achieve acceptance rates of alpha = 0.68 at draft length k=2 under greedy decoding, while sequential hybrids yield only alpha = 0.038 -- an 18x gap attributable to how each architecture integrates its components. The property is scale-invariant: Falcon-H1 at 3B reproduces the rates observed at 0.5B. We further show that perplexity degradation from a companion ablation study predicts speculative viability without running speculative decoding: a 3.15x ratio (Falcon) maps to alpha = 0.37 at k=4, while 81.96x (Qwen) maps to alpha = 0.019. For sequential hybrids, generic LayerSkip achieves 12x higher acceptance rates than the component-aware strategy. The composition pattern of hybrid models -- not merely the presence of alternative components -- determines whether component-level self-speculation is viable.
====================================================================================================
2609.24197v1 | 2026-09-21 | updated 2026-09-21
TITLE: H-Spec: Parallel Speculative Decoding Without a Drafter-Side KV Cache
AUTH: Weifan Jiang, Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata, Megan Flynn, Reed Meyerson, Zhenting Qi, Tianyu Wu, Eldar Kurtic, Minlan Yu ...
COMMENT: 22 pages, 12 figures
ABS: Speculative decoding losslessly accelerates large language model inference by having a lightweight draft model predict future tokens for verification by the target model. Recent block diffusion drafters further reduce drafting latency by predicting multiple tokens in parallel. However, existing block drafters project target hidden states at every input position into a separate drafter-side KV cache, incurring per-request memory and KV-write overhead that grow with concurrency; directly reusing target KVs in place removes this cache but fails to sustain draft quality throughout the block. We propose a hybrid target-context injection method that complements direct target KV reuse with target hidden states only at the last input position, requiring no separate drafter-side KV cache. Building on this design, we propose H-Spec, a hybrid Mamba-attention parallel drafter that consumes the two target-context sources through complementary modules. Mamba modules are initialized with projected last-token target hidden states, while attention modules reuse target KVs in place. Despite its recurrent formulation, Mamba's parallel scan allows H-Spec to preserve block-parallel drafting. Across three target models and diverse tasks, H-Spec improves over the best baseline by 5.0--13.3% in mean accepted length and 5.3--12.6% in batch-size-1 inter-token latency speedup. Under concurrent serving, H-Spec consistently achieves higher throughput while maintaining lower KV cache utilization than baselines across evaluated concurrency levels.
====================================================================================================
2607.21535v1 | 2026-07-23 | updated 2026-07-23
TITLE: Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context
AUTH: Alagappan Valliappan
COMMENT: 25 pages, 2 figures, 11 tables
ABS: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.
====================================================================================================
2609.23900v3 | 2026-09-20 | updated 2026-10-04
TITLE: LumoTree: Path-Parallel Speculative Verification for Hybrid Language Models
AUTH: Zhiyuan Ma
COMMENT: 16 pages, 3 figures. v3: measurements re-taken with corrected per-path penalty histories in the tree sampler
ABS: Tree speculative decoding for recurrent-hybrid language models requires each accepted path to maintain consistent recurrent state, convolution history, and attention caches. We present LumoTree, a GPU serving design that coordinates verification and commitment through a shared tree descriptor. The verifier processes independent paths in parallel and reuses recurrent state tiles across local updates. Boundary states connect dependent paths. Accepted-path replay publishes the selected continuation into native running state, alongside coordinated convolution gathering and attention-cache remapping. Fused selection, device-resident acceptance, graph replay, and tree-aware attention integrate this organization into the serving cycle. The design separates temporary branch computation from persistent request state while retaining native prefix-cache interfaces. We evaluate numerical behavior, serving performance, and coding-agent outcomes on NVIDIA DGX Spark.
====================================================================================================
2607.16673v1 | 2026-07-18 | updated 2026-07-18
TITLE: SpecLA: Efficient Speculative Decoding for Linear-Attention Models
AUTH: Zhibin Wang, Xuying Han, Zhaohua Yang, Fuliang Liu, Xue Li, Rong Gu, Sheng Zhong, Chen Tian
ABS: Linear-attention models replace the growing KV cache with recurrent states, but autoregressive decoding still reads, updates, and writes these states one token at a time. Speculative decoding can reduce this cost by verifying several draft tokens in one target pass, yet existing speculative systems are designed for Transformer KV caches. For stateful linear-attention targets, verification must follow recurrent dependencies across chains and branches, acceptance must update only the accepted state trajectory, and the drafter must avoid submitting candidates that waste stateful verification work. This paper presents SpecLA, a speculative decoding runtime for stateful linear-attention models. SpecLA verifies chains and trees with topology-aware kernels, stores compact factors produced during verification to recover accepted states, and uses confidence pruning plus a target-aligned EAGLE-style drafter to feed useful candidates to the verifier. On an NVIDIA H100 with a public GDN-1.3B target, SpecLA achieves up to 1.70x end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding.
====================================================================================================
2605.19049v1 | 2026-05-18 | updated 2026-05-18
TITLE: KVBuffer: IO-aware Serving for Linear Attention
AUTH: Longwei Zou, Lin Zhong
ABS: Linear attention has recently gained significant attention for long-context inference due to its constant decoding cost with respect to context length. However, existing serving systems typically serve linear attention by recurrently computing and updating a large linear attention state in every decoding step. Since the state is much larger than the per-token key and value, recurrent decoding incurs substantial memory access and becomes inefficient for serving linear attention. In this paper, we propose KVBuffer, an IO-aware serving mechanism for linear attention. By buffering recent keys and values, KVBuffer enables serving systems to compute linear attention outputs in more flexible and memory-efficient ways. For decoding, KVBuffer enables chunkwise computation, which reduces average memory access and decoding latency by deferring state updates and applying them in batch. For speculative decoding, KVBuffer verifies draft tokens in parallel and avoids storing temporary states. For short contexts, KVBuffer computes attention outputs directly from buffered keys and values, without creating or updating the linear attention state. We implement KVBuffer in SGLang for Qwen3-Next. Our evaluations show that KVBuffer can reduce linear attention decoding latency by up to 45.17% and increase the maximum number of serving requests by 5x for speculative decoding when verifying four draft tokens.

TITLE: Just Let Linear States Forget the Distant Past: Prefix Caching via Suffix Replay for Hybrid LLMs
AUTH: Yirui Liu, Ruoling Qi, Xuaner Wu, Yuxin Jin, Jian Chen, Penghang Liu, Yafei Huang, Jiawei Shao ...
ABS: Hybrid LLMs interleave full-attention layers with linear-attention layers to reduce long-context inference cost, but this structure complicates prefix caching. Full-attention KV caches are token-addressable, whereas linear-attention layers maintain recurrent states that cannot be rolled back to arbitrary prefix boundaries. Existing systems materialize recurrent-state checkpoints, restricting prefix reuse to checkpoint-aligned positions. We present SuffixReplay, the first prefix caching system that lets hybrid LLMs reuse cached prefixes at every cache-supported page boundary without materializing recurrent-state checkpoints. Our key insight is to just let linear states forget the distant past. Modern linear-attention mechanisms use recurrent decay and gating to attenuate the influence of old inputs. Therefore, instead of checkpointing every prefix boundary, SuffixReplay approximates the state at a matched boundary by replaying only a recent suffix of the layer's input hidden states, which we retain as anchors. At the algorithmic level, SuffixReplay combines layer-wise and token-wise anchor sparsity with a bounded replay budget to control storage, computation, and quality. At the system level, it uses an independently managed anchor sidecar and a pipelined replay path to overlap anchor movement and state reconstruction with the native serving pipeline. We evaluate SuffixReplay on three hybrid LLMs: OLMo-Hybrid-7B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.6-27B-FP8. Across these models, SuffixReplay retains 91.4-100% of full-prefill quality on average across LongBench and RULER, while using only 0.36-0.51x the amortized per-token storage of SGLang's default 8192-token checkpoint cache. Integrated into SGLang, SuffixReplay reduces median TTFT by 15-70% on branching workloads, sustains 2.3-4.3x SGLang's throughput when the working set exceeds HBM, and matches SGLang on high-hit continuation traffic.

TITLE: SpecMamba: Accelerating Mamba Inference on FPGA with Speculative Decoding
AUTH: Linfeng Zhong, Songqiang Xu, Huifeng Wen, Tong Xie, Qingyu Guo, Yuan Wang, Meng Li
COMMENT: Accepted by ICCAD'25
ABS: The growing demand for efficient long-sequence modeling on edge devices has propelled widespread adoption of State Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba, due to their superior computational efficiency and scalability. As its autoregressive generation process remains memory-bound, speculative decoding has been proposed that incorporates draft model generation and target model verification. However, directly applying speculative decoding to SSMs faces three key challenges: (1) hidden state backtracking difficulties, (2) tree-based parallel verification incompatibility, and (3) hardware workload mismatch. To address these challenges, we propose SpecMamba, the first FPGA-based accelerator for Mamba with speculative decoding, which features system, algorithm, and hardware co-design. At the system level, we present a memory-aware hybrid backtracking strategy to coordinate both models. At the algorithm level, we propose first-in-first-out (FIFO)-based tree verification with tiling to minimize memory access. At the hardware level, we customize a dataflow that computes linear layers in parallel and SSM layers in series to enable maximal overlapping. Implemented on AMD FPGA platforms (VHK158 and VCK190), SpecMamba achieves a 2.27x speedup over GPU baselines and a 2.85x improvement compared to prior FPGA solutions, while demonstrating 5.41x and 1.26x higher energy efficiency, respectively.

TITLE: HYPIC: Accelerating Hybrid-Attention LLM Serving with Position-Independent Caching
AUTH: Yifei Liu, Juntong Wu, Yang Liu, Junhao Hu, Minghao Li, Xiaoxu Chen, Weihang Chen
ABS: In retrieval-augmented generation and agentic LLM serving, prompts are assembled from independent segments into long contexts, making the prefill stage dominate per-request cost. However, they cannot coexist: applying existing PIC methods to hybrid-attention models breaks down because per-token KV-cache reuse primitives do not transfer to the per-request recurrent state. For linear-attention layers, we identify the segment-cumulative transition operator as the missing algebraic primitive and cache it alongside each segment's zero-start end-state, enabling near-exact and constant-time composition of independently cached segments. For the remaining full-attention layers, existing PIC methods also fail because linear layers do not expose the per-token hidden states needed for selective recomputation. We show that the largest deviations concentrate at segment beginnings and construct a small seam window that propagates hidden states through the hybrid-attention stack to repair cross-segment attention. Finally, Hypic introduces segment parallelism, which exploits PIC's segment-level self-containment to parallelize cache-miss prefill across instances, turning long cold requests into an accelerable workload. TITLE: Super Apriel: One Checkpoint, Many Speeds

TITLE: RAD: Redundancy-Aware Distillation for Hybrid Models via Self-Speculative Decoding
AUTH: Yuichiro Hoshino, Hideyuki Tachibana, Muneyoshi Inahara, Hiroto Takegawa
COMMENT: 26 pages

TITLE: STree: Speculative Tree Decoding for Hybrid State-Space Models
AUTH: Yangchao Wu, Zongyue Qin, Alex Wong, Stefano Soatto
ABS: Speculative decoding is a technique to leverage hardware concurrency in order to enable multiple steps of token generation in a single forward pass, thus improving the efficiency of large-scale autoregressive (AR) Transformer models. TITLE: Sparse Prefix Caching for Hybrid and Recurrent LLM Serving
AUTH: Mikhail Shirokikh, Sergey Nikolenko

AUTH: Linfeng Zhong, Songqiang Xu, Huifeng Wen, Tong Xie, Qingyu Guo, Yuan Wang, Meng Li
COMMENT: Accepted by ICCAD'25
ABS: The growing demand for efficient long-sequence modeling on edge devices has propelled widespread adoption of State Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba, due to their superior computational efficiency and scalability. TITLE: Tail-Replay: Escaping the Curse of Linear Attention in Prefix Caching for Hybrid LLMs
AUTH: Yirui Liu, Ruoling Qi, Xuaner Wu, Penghang Liu, Jian Chen

TITLE: Mamba Drafters for Speculative Decoding
AUTH: Daewon Choi, Seunghyuk Oh, Saket Dingliwal, Jihoon Tack, Kyuyoung Kim, Woomin Song, Seojin Kim, Insu Han ...
ABS: Speculative decoding has emerged as a promising approach to accelerating large language model (LLM) generation using a fast drafter while maintaining alignment with the target model's distribution. However, existing approaches face a trade-off: external drafters offer flexibility but can suffer from slower drafting, while self-speculation methods use drafters tailored to the target model but require re-training. In this paper, we introduce novel drafters based on Mamba, a state-of-the-art state space model (SSM), as a solution that combines the best aspects of both approaches. By leveraging the linear structure of SSMs, our approach avoids the quadratic complexity inherent in traditional Transformer-based methods, enabling faster drafting and lower memory usage while maintaining the flexibility to work across different target models. We further enhance efficiency with a novel test-time tree search algorithm for generating high-quality draft candidates. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that Mamba-based drafters not only outperform existing external drafting methods but are also comparable to state-of-the-art self-speculation approaches while using less memory and maintaining their cross-model adaptability.
====================================================================================================
2607.04244v2 | 2026-07-05 | updated 2026-07-07
TITLE: Quantize the Target, Quantize the Drafter: Efficient Inference with Qwen3.5-4B
AUTH: Jaeyeon Kim, Jewon Lee, Bo-Kyeong Kim
COMMENT: All authors contributed equally. Our submission to Efficient Qwen Competition, ICML 2026 Workshop on AdaptFM
ABS: This report describes our approach to the Efficient Qwen Competition, where the goal is to enable low-latency serving of Qwen3.5-4B on a resource-constrained NVIDIA A10G GPU. Our system combines a quantized target model with speculative decoding. To recover accuracy, we apply quantization-aware distillation to the target model while retaining the original quantization grid. To speed up decoding, a block-diffusion drafter specialized for the quantized target model is trained using a two-stage procedure: first learning from the high-precision target and then adapting to the low-precision target. Because the drafter is invoked at every speculative decoding step, we further reduce its overhead with quantization and sliding-window attention, preserving draft-token acceptance while improving long-context decoding latency. As a result, our submission achieves a 6.978$\times$ average speedup over the baseline while satisfying the required quality thresholds, ranking 3rd overall. We hope these results provide useful insights for practical LLM inference. The code and resources are available at https://github.com/nota-github/adaptfm-quant-dflash
====================================================================================================
2609.33184v1 | 2026-09-27 | updated 2026-09-27
TITLE: Resource-Efficient Speculative Decoding for Long-Context LLM Serving
AUTH: Fei Li, Song Liu, Shiqiang Nie, Jinyu Wang, Weiguo Wu
COMMENT: 14 pages, 10 figures
ABS: Speculative decoding reduces sequential Target model calls by verifying multiple tokens from the Draft model in parallel. Yet KV Cache growth limits long-context serving under constrained GPU memory. Offloading KV to CPU memory relieves this pressure. However, existing offloading schemes restore the full KV history before attention and fail to fully exploit the benefits of KV sharing across queries within a verification round. Existing parallel speculative decoding methods also overlook idle GPU compute capacity while memory-bandwidth-bound Target verification waits for historical KV. We present SpecStream, a speculative decoding system that begins verification without waiting for the full KV history to be restored and exploits compute bubbles during KV transfers for concurrent drafting on the same GPUs. It offloads only Target-committed history, keeping candidate rollback local to the GPUs. Each streamed KV chunk serves all queries in the round, with online softmax preserving full attention. ## Snakes and Ladders: Accelerating SSM Inference with Speculative Decoding

**Authors and venue:** Wu, Y., Dukler, Y., Trager, M., Achille, A., Xia, W. & Soatto, S. (2024). It was published in the Proceedings of The 4th NeurIPS Efficient Natural Language and Speech Processing Workshop, PMLR 262:292-304. Amazon Science also hosts the paper.

**The problem:** Speculative decoding is a method for accelerating inference in large language models (LLMs) by predicting multiple tokens using a smaller 'draft model' and validating them against the larger 'base model.' When a draft token is wrong, the model has to go back to the last correct token. This is straightforward in autoregressive Transformer architectures since their state is a sliding window of past tokens. However, State Space Models (SSMs) have linear inference complexity, but they maintain a separate Markov state that makes backtracking non-trivial. In Transformers, the key-value caches store all the necessary information to easily backtrack to the state after the last correctly drafted token. In SSMs, the required intermediate states are not instantiated in global memory and cannot be easily recovered from the final state. As a result, the correct state must be recomputed.

**The two proposed methods:**
- **Activation Replay:** it stores partial computation from past states that facilitate state backtracking.
- **Joint Attainment and Advancement:** it tracks a desired state and assigns additional computation to predict the next verified state jointly as part of the next forward pass.

The authors also wrote a hardware-aware fused kernel that avoid[s] storing the large SSM state out to HBM at each step, which reduces the cost of memory transfer.

**Results:**
- The methods can produce 6 tokens for 1.47× the cost of one, corresponding to an average 1.82× wall-clock speed-up on three different benchmarks using a simple n-gram for drafting.
- As model size increases, relative overhead of speculation and verification decreases: Scaling from 1.3B parameters to 13B reduces relative overhead from 1.98× to 1.22×.
- Unlike Transformers, speculative decoding in SSMs can be easily applied to batches of sequences, allowing dynamic allocation of resources to fill gaps in compute utilization and thereby improving efficiency and throughput with variable inference traffic.

**Follow-up work:** Several later papers cite it. One is Yangchao Wu, Zongyue Qin, Alex Wong, and Stefano Soatto. 2025. STree: Speculative Tree Decoding for Hybrid State-Space Models. The 2026 LumoTree paper says that Snakes and Ladders introduces activation replay for SSM speculative decoding, and STree also uses replay to recover continuation state. A review of SpecLA, a speculative decoding system for linear-attention models, criticizes it because they cite Snakes and Ladders and STree for SSM speculative decoding but don't compare against them.

Here's what the search turned up on speculative decoding with tree-based verification for state space models like Mamba.

**1. STree: Speculative Tree Decoding for Hybrid State Space Models (OpenReview)**
This is the closest match to your query.
- **The problem:** Speculative decoding has already been applied to SSMs, but existing approaches do not use tree-based verification, since current SSMs lack the means to compute a token tree efficiently.
- **What they propose:** The first scalable algorithm to perform tree-based speculative decoding in state-space models (SSMs) and hybrid architectures of SSMs and Transformer layers. It works by exploiting the structure of accumulated state transition matrices to facilitate tree-based speculative decoding with minimal overhead relative to current SSM implementations.
- **Why it's needed:** Modern SSM implementations (Mamba, Mamba2) scan causally through all past tokens to get the state, with no way to specify a tree structure. They also need one state per input sequence in the batch, so memory use explodes when the tree is unrolled.
- **Relation to Mamba2:** The authors call their method a generalization of the matrix transformation form of SSM in Mamba2.
- **Scaling:** As model size grows, STree's relative overhead drops from 2.04x to 1.26x. One caveat: the 7B, 13B and 23B models in that test were initialized with random weights to measure runtime, since no pretrained models of those sizes exist.
- **Code:** https://github.com/wyc1997/stree

**2. SpecMamba: Accelerating Mamba Inference on FPGA with Speculative Decoding (arXiv 2509.19873)**
- The paper names three key challenges in applying speculative decoding to SSMs: (1) hidden state backtracking difficulties, (2) tree-based parallel verification incompatibility, and (3) hardware workload mismatch.
- It's the first FPGA-based accelerator for Mamba with speculative decoding, using system, algorithm, and hardware co-design.

**3. Mamba Drafters for Speculative Decoding (EMNLP 2025 Findings / arXiv 2506.01206)**
- This paper flips the setup: it uses Mamba-based drafters to combine the strengths of both external drafters and self-speculation.
- The Mamba drafter keeps decoding speed and memory use nearly constant, while Transformer-based drafters like EAGLE need much more memory as context length grows.
- It also covers efficient state caching during tree-structured drafting.

**Note on dates:** The STree OpenReview page is dated October 2025, which looks like an ICLR 2026 submission timeline. The search results don't confirm whether it was accepted.

I found several recent papers and engineering threads (July–October 2026) on this. They all deal with the same issue: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers update their recurrent state in place, so rejected draft tokens can't just be dropped. Systems either save a copy (snapshot) of the state at each draft position, or rebuild only the accepted state afterward.

## The core problem
- In hybrid models, most layers are linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet, GDN) layers carrying a small fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value (KV) cache. This makes ordinary decoding memory-efficient, but hurts speculative decoding.
- Without auxiliary state snapshots, rejected speculative draft tokens permanently contaminate recurrent memory.
- Decoding these layers still has a cost: each token still reads, updates, and writes a dense recurrent state. That makes verifying several draft tokens in one pass appealing.

## Current default: one snapshot per draft position
- The current default in both vLLM (storeall in our figures) and SGLang: one recurrent-state snapshot per draft position, rolled back by indexing to the accepted one. Rollback is free; memory scales with draft size and snapshots cannot be shared across tree branches. As a result, a wide, high-acceptance tree becomes memory-infeasible.
- **llama.cpp (PR #28118):** for Qwen3-Next-style hybrids, speculative decoding must checkpoint and restore the full recurrent state every round. Copying that state to host memory on AMD Strix Halo was ~600 ms of each ~825 ms round, a constant ~73% overhead that makes speculative decoding a net loss despite high draft acceptance. The fix keeps the per-round snapshots on the device.
- **SceneWorks inference (PR #1032):** keeps a preallocated ring buffer for each linear layer. Every forward writes the state after each of its last slots tokens in place, so rollback needs no replay forward pass.

## Approaches that skip snapshots
- **TreeWY (arXiv 2608.20961):** Using a tree-structured WY transform of the gated delta rule, we compute every draft node's output with a single triangular solve and reconstruct only the one accepted state on commit, storing a small pseudo-value matrix instead of per-node states. It was tested on Qwen3.5 35B and 397B. The authors report that it cuts speculative recurrent-state memory and KV-cache pressure at identical acceptance length, turning the freed HBM into higher throughput and much lower time-to-first-token (TTFT) wherever memory binds, and costing a few percent where it does not. Wider trees are now affordable, though not yet a throughput win. One reviewer calls the memory claim incomplete because Eq (3) needs the draft keys and the paper never says where they live. The reviewer's suggested test is relevant to your batch-size question: measure peak HBM during a verified draft while sweeping draft-tree width at fixed batch size.
- **ReplaySSM** (cited in TreeWY): keeps a checkpoint plus a short cached history and defers materializing the state until a periodic flush, so state is written far less often than every draft step. It covers Mamba2 and GDN, and the implementation linked in the RFC is chain-only (not a tree).
- **SpecLA (arXiv 2607.16673):** its verification kernels can keep recurrent state tiles on-chip for chains, use a tree-masked factorized form for branches, and commit accepted states from compact factors rather than snapshots or replays. It reports up to 1.70x end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding on a 1.3B GDN model on an H100. A reviewer notes an internal contradiction about which model was actually measured.
- **LumoTree / GDN Tree-Scan (arXiv 2609.23900):** The verifier processes independent paths in parallel and reuses recurrent state tiles across local updates. Boundary states connect dependent paths. It was evaluated on Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 on a DGX Spark. The authors argue that neither a fast isolated recurrent kernel nor low transient state memory alone determines user-visible latency.

## Batch size
None of these results directly measures how verification cost changes with batch size. What they suggest: snapshot memory grows with draft size, and therefore with batch × draft length. Snapshot-free methods mainly pay off where memory is the bottleneck (high concurrency or long context). Where memory isn't tight, TreeWY costs a few percent. If you want, I can search specifically for batch-size scaling numbers, such as the vLLM ReplaySSM RFC benchmarks.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

content.content:
# TreeWY (arXiv:2608.20961v1): extraction

## (1) How vLLM and SGLang store and roll back GDN state today

**Full-state snapshotting (the default)**
- The paper says this is the default in both vLLM and SGLang. In its figures, vLLM's default is labeled "storeall" (config value `"store_all"`).
- It keeps the committed state plus one full snapshot per draft position. That is k+1 blocks per sequence per GDN layer for a k-token chain, or N+1 for an N-node tree.
- Rollback works by indexing to the accepted snapshot. Rollback is free, but memory grows with draft size, and the snapshots are "unshareable across branches."
- At k=3 this is 4× the committed state: 120 MiB/seq for 35B and 360 MiB/seq for 397B.
- The SGLang citation notes "Hybrid state pool as of v0.5.16, 2026."

**ReplaySSM (Dao AI Lab + NVIDIA)**
- It stores a checkpoint plus a short cached history and only materializes state at a periodic flush.
- Inside the verify window it solves the same triangular system as TreeWY.
- It covers both Mamba2 and GDN. The implementation linked in the RFC handles chains only, not trees.
- Sources cited:
  - Blog: "ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State" (2026)
  - vLLM RFC #47572 and PR #47576
  - TensorRT-LLM PR #14203
  - SGLang port, opt-in: Issue #28511 (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/28511), by Y. Luo

**`num_speculative_blocks`** does not appear anywhere in the page.

**TreeWY's own vLLM options** (a fork, not upstreamed):
- `mamba_state_commit="reconstruct"` replaces `"store_all"`.
- `draft_tree_widths` sets the per-level branching factor.

## (2) Related work on SSM, linear-attention and hybrid speculation

- **STree** (Wu et al., arXiv:2505.14969, 2025): tree verification for Mamba2 only. It depends on the scalar decay becoming a cheap cumulative sum, which "does _not_ exist for GDN's non-commuting matrix transition."
- **Snakes and Ladders** (Wu et al., NeurIPS ENLSP Workshop 2024): cited alongside STree.
- **Bole** (Wang et al., arXiv:2608.01651, Aug 2026, concurrent):
  - A tree-structured closed form for hybrid-attention recurrences, built on SGLang.
  - Reports "82–99× transient-memory reduction and 3.4–7.7× faster tree verification."
  - No code is linked, so there is no head-to-head comparison.
- **ReplaySSM**: see section 1.
- **Background work cited:**
  - Speculative decoding: Leviathan et al. (ICML 2023); Chen et al. (arXiv:2302.01318)
  - Medusa trees: arXiv:2401.10774
  - Gated DeltaNet: ICLR 2025
  - DeltaNet chain WY transform: arXiv:2406.06484. TreeWY generalizes this transform to trees.

## (3) Setup and results

**Setup**
- Hardware: B200 GPUs, 178 GiB HBM each.
- Models and parallelism: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at TP1 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B at TP8.
- Engine: vLLM with prefix caching disabled.
- Draft method: depth-3 MTP draft chain, greedy drafting and verification.
- GPU memory utilization (gmu): 0.6, 0.75, 0.9.
- Concurrency: 1, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256.
- BurstGPT instead sweeps arrival rate: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 req/s.
- Workloads: ShareGPT, spec-bench, BurstGPT, and synthetic balanced-chat, generation-heavy and summarize-heavy.
- 175 matched points in total. Compute was about 85 GPU-hours.

**Memory baseline**
- KV cache costs 20 KiB/token (35B) and 30 KiB/token (397B).
- GDN state costs 30 MiB/seq (35B) and 90 MiB/seq (397B).

**Correctness**
- The closed form matches the recurrence to about 1e-15 (fp64) and 1e-7 (fp32).
- Acceptance length versus baseline: mean |Δ| = 0.039, max 0.33.

**Main results**
- Peak KV usage is 2–3× lower.
- Preemptions: 1365 vs. 2531. Only 51 of TreeWY's are at 397B, against 909 for storeall.
- Where memory binds: up to 1.49× throughput and about 40× lower p99 TTFT (683 vs. 27489 ms at 35B, gmu 0.6, concurrency 128).
- Where memory does not bind: throughput is 0.97–0.99×.
- Table 1 at concurrency 256:

| Model (gmu) | Throughput | TTFT | TPOT | Admitted-batch ratio b |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35B (0.6) | 1.40 | 3.97 | 0.60 | 2.50 |
| 397B (0.75) | 1.15 | 3.35 | 0.90 | 1.24 |

- The knee where TreeWY starts winning moves with the budget: concurrency 128 at gmu 0.6, 256 at 0.75, and never at 0.9.

**Verification cost versus batch size**
- The paper has no direct kernel-timing sweep.
- Appendix C instead correlates the TPOT penalty with the running-batch ratio (Pearson r = −0.88).
- At the 31 saturated points, TPOT is 0.83× but end-to-end latency improves 1.17×. Elsewhere TPOT is 0.98×.
- At concurrency 1, TPOT is 0.94 (Table 1).

**Verification cost versus number of draft tokens (tree width)**
- Acceptance length rises with tree size: 3.23 for (1,1,1) with N=3, up to 3.58 for (3,3,3) with N=39.
- Storeall's per-request cost grows from 4 to 40 blocks, while TreeWY stays at 1 block.
- Trees are not a throughput win: "a wider tree pushes N+1 tokens per step through the target and runs piecewise."

**Against ReplaySSM (35B)**
- ReplaySSM leads on throughput: 1.12–1.20× versus TreeWY's 0.99–1.08×.
- At concurrency 256, the per-token cost is 1.295× for TreeWY versus 1.035× for ReplaySSM.
- Throughput there is 1.192 versus 1.376.
- On BurstGPT at 64 req/s, the TTFT improvement is 10.72× versus 10.20×.

## (4) ROCm/AMD

The paper says nothing about ROCm or AMD. All runs are on NVIDIA B200, and the kernel is described as "Triton" and "CUDA-graph-capturable."

## (5) Stated limitations

- Real trees (width > 1) need a non-causal mask that cannot be replayed from a CUDA graph. vLLM then falls back to piecewise capture, which also evicts the GDN mixer from graphs.
- Trees must be scheduled atomically. A tree that does not fit the per-step token budget skips speculation rather than being truncated.
- Output is not bit-identical to the baseline, only within bf16 tolerance.
- Throughput is a few percent lower when memory is not the constraint.
- Trees are "enabled and correct, not as a speedup."
- There is a per-step gap to ReplaySSM. The paper attributes it to materializing state on every commit, but this is an untested hypothesis.
- There is no Bole comparison, only one model family was tested, the work is not upstreamed, and prefix caching was disabled throughout.

Web search results for query: "ReplaySSM "Cache SSM Inputs, Not State" speculative decoding"

Links: [{"title":"ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State | Tri Dao","url":"https://tridao.me/blog/2026/replayssm/"},{"title":"ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State | Dao AI Lab","url":"https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/"},{"title":"GitHub - Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM · GitHub","url":"https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM"},{"title":"SketchSSM: Write to the Full State, Read from a Compact Sketch","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2609.33051"}]

ReplaySSM is a 2026 method from Tri Dao's lab (Dao AI Lab). It speeds up decoding in hybrid models that mix attention with SSM layers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. A later paper credits it to Z. Liou and T. Dao.

**Main idea**
- ReplaySSM caches recent SSM inputs in a small ring buffer instead of writing the recurrent state back to HBM every decode step. It reconstructs states on the fly and writes back only when the buffer is full.
- This helps because SSM decoding is memory-bound, so reducing memory traffic directly improves latency. A "flush" costs more since it summarizes a chunk of recent inputs into the state and writes the full state back once, but this cost is amortized across the whole window.

**How it helps speculative decoding**
- The draft tokens are kept as raw cached inputs. Because it doesn't perform the irreversible summarization per step, rolling back rejected draft tokens only requires removing their buffer entries. That means there is no full state to restore for each rejected token, and no per-token state copy to keep in memory for recovery.
- During speculative decoding, a flush only summarizes the committed cached inputs into the state. The current step's speculative tokens are not summarized, since rejected ones must still be rolled back. The accepted tokens remain in the buffer as the cached inputs for the next decoding step.
- Thanks to the ring buffer, a rollback becomes purely a pointer move. The ring buffer is also important for tree-based speculative decoding, where accepted tokens are no longer contiguous in the buffer.

**Results**
- The authors tested it on two hybrid families with different SSM layers: Nemotron-3 (Mamba-2) and Qwen3.5 (GDN). It is implemented in vLLM, and both families use their MTP heads as the drafter.
- ReplaySSM speeds up standard decoding by up to 1.43x. vLLM's existing speculative decoding falls below standard-decoding throughput at serving batch sizes, while ReplaySSM speculative decoding delivers 1.87–1.96x. Speculative window = 4 and all models are NVFP4 on B300.

**Code**
The open-source vLLM fork is at github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM. It includes separate speculative-decoding kernels for Mamba-2 (selective_state_update_replayssm_spec.py — speculative decode on a circular buffer) and for GDN (gdn_replayssm_spec_decode.py).

**Follow-up work**
A later paper, SketchSSM, points out a remaining gap: ReplaySSM amortizes state updates by buffering keys and values, but each new query still requires a full-state read even though the state remains unchanged between state updates. SketchSSM addresses this by approximating those state reads with a compact sketch.

Sources: the blog posts at tridao.me/blog/2026/replayssm/ and dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/.

**Title:** "[RFC]: ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs instead of state for faster standard and speculative decode (Mamba2 + GDN)" (Issue #47572, vllm-project/vllm)
**Author:** Johnny-Liou
**Status:** Open (label: RFC; no assignees or milestone)
**Created:** July 3, 2026

## The Problem

- **Decode bottleneck:** In hybrid models, the SSM/linear-attention layers dominate decode latency at short-to-medium output lengths. They are memory-bound because every step reads and rewrites the full recurrent state.
- **Speculative decoding rollback:** The SSM state update can't be undone. Once a token is folded into the state, it can't be removed. To allow rollback, vLLM currently keeps a separate recurrent state for each draft token. This costs roughly "(1 + num\_spec)× the state" in HBM footprint plus extra memory traffic, which hurts both latency and maximum concurrency.

## Proposed Design

- **Checkpoint plus ring buffer:** Each request keeps one checkpoint state S0 and a ring buffer of recent SSM inputs.
- **Flush steps:** Once every L steps, the cached inputs are folded into the checkpoint.
- **Other steps:** The output is computed directly from the checkpoint plus cached inputs, without materializing the state. These steps are read-only apart from a small input append.
- **What is cached:** Only state-building inputs (e.g., dt/B/x for Mamba2). The output read vector (Mamba2 C, GDN q) comes from current activations.
- **Rollback:** Undoing rejected tokens becomes a ring-buffer pointer move. Per-step rollback cost drops from O(T) to O(1), where T = num\_spec\_tokens + 1.
- **Parallel verification:** A draft window is verified in a single pass instead of a serial recurrence.
- **Spec-decode flush rule:** Flush when `history + T > B`, with the ring buffer sized to B + T. This differs slightly from the blog post.
- **Triangular solve:** The page doesn't mention a "replay/triangular solve." It only describes reconstructing the state from cached inputs.

**Integration:**
- Triton kernels; the existing `causal_conv1d_update` is reused unchanged.
- Caches are extra tensors on the paged mamba state, indexed by physical block id.
- CUDA graphs are supported via two device-routed launches (verify and flush).
- Everything is opt-in, and with the feature off the path is byte-identical to the baseline.

**Config flags (all default off):**
- `--use-replayssm`
- `--use-replayssm-spec` (requires `--mamba-cache-mode none`)
- `--replayssm-buffer-len` (default 16)
- `--replayssm-route` (temporary)

**Validation:** Per-kernel checks against an exact reference, prefill-vs-decode equivalence, `check_logprobs_close` parity, and GSM8K acceptance-length match.

## Benchmarks

**Standard decode** (whole-model per-step speedup, fp32 state, buffer length 16):

| Model (SSM, GPU) | bs 1 | bs 32 | bs 128 | bs 512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Nano-4B (Mamba2, H100) | 0.99 | 1.17 | 1.40 | 1.55 |
| Qwen3.5-4B (GDN, H100) | 0.99 | 1.08 | 1.21 | 1.31 |
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2, B300) | 0.98 | 1.10 | 1.27 | 1.67 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN, B300) | 0.98 | 1.07 | 1.14 | 1.20 |

**Speculative decode** (B300, MTP drafter, (B, T) = (16, 4)):

| Model | Comparison | bs 1 | bs 32 | bs 256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2) | vs. native spec | 1.09 | 1.07 | 1.88 |
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2) | vs. no-spec AR | 2.12 | 1.90 | 2.21 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN) | vs. native spec | 0.99 | 1.19 | 1.80 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN) | vs. no-spec AR | 1.90 | 1.93 | 1.85 |

- Gains are largest at big batch sizes. Small batches are overhead-bound, not memory-bound.
- **Memory savings:** The design removes the per-draft-token state storage, but no specific memory figures are given. Full numbers are deferred to the draft PR.

## Links

- Draft PR: vLLM #47576
- Related feature request: #46187 (assigned to the authors)
- Concurrent TensorRT-LLM PR: #14203
- Dao AI Lab blog post and the ReplaySSM reference repository
- The work is a Dao AI Lab and NVIDIA collaboration.

## Work in Progress and Open Questions

**Work in progress:**
- Tensor-parallel tests
- Evaluation with fp16/fp8 state
- A possible precision benefit, since the checkpoint is re-quantized about L× less often

**Open questions:**
- Proposed rollout order: Mamba2 standard, then GDN standard, then speculative decode for both.
- Whether the caches should be appended to the mamba state or allocated separately.

## Comments

- **ZJY0516 (member), Aug 1:** Asked how ReplaySSM interacts with prefix caching plus spec decoding.
- **Johnny-Liou, Aug 1:** Said this won't be in the first spec-decode PR. The idea would be to store a checkpoint plus a few ring-cache tokens (e.g., a checkpoint at token 98 plus two cached tokens) and prepend those tokens during prefill on a cache hit.
- **ZJY0516, Aug 3:** Pushed back, saying it "would add a lot of complexity to the KV cache manager, and the ring cache isn't managed by it now."
- An unrelated commit in the jieen1/BlackweLLM repo references the issue.

## ROCm/AMD

There is no mention of ROCm or AMD. All results are on NVIDIA H100 and B300.

# ReplaySSM PR #47576 (vllm-project/vllm)

**Title:** "[Kernel] ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs instead of state for faster standard and speculative decode (Mamba2 + GDN)"

**Author:** Johnny-Liou (Dao AI Lab × NVIDIA collaboration; RFC #47572)

**Status:** Open, marked as **Draft**. It has 19 commits and carries the `needs-rebase` label because of merge conflicts.

**Dates:** Created July 3, 2026. It has not been merged, so there is no merge date. Commits continued through July 20, and the PR was referenced as late as October 8, 2026.

**Follow-ups:** The author plans to land the work in stages. The split PRs are #48792 (GDN standard decode), #49847 (Mamba2 spec decode) and #49887 (GDN spec decode).

## What it changes

**Core idea:** Decode is memory-bound, and writing the full recurrent state back to HBM every step dominates the traffic. ReplaySSM instead keeps three things:
- a checkpoint state S₀
- a small ring buffer of recent SSM inputs
- full-state writebacks only on periodic "flushes"

**Config flags** (all off by default, so the baseline path is unchanged):
- `--use-replayssm`: standard decode for Mamba2 and GDN.
- `--replayssm-route`: chooses `output_only` (default) or `state_and_output`. It applies to Mamba2 only, and the alternate route will be removed later.
- `--use-replayssm-spec`: speculative decode. It requires spec decoding plus `--mamba-cache-mode none`.
- `--replayssm-buffer-len`: the history block B, default 16.

**New Triton kernels:**

| Path | Kernel(s) |
|---|---|
| Mamba2 standard | `selective_state_update_replayssm_output_only` / `…_state_and_output` |
| Mamba2 spec | `selective_state_update_replayssm_spec`, plus `commit_replayssm_spec` / `reset_*` |
| GDN standard | `fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_replayssm` |
| GDN spec | `gdn_replayssm_spec_decode`, plus commit/reset kernels |
| Shared | `get_replayssm_config`, which auto-detects the hardware |

**Integration points:**
- The kernels are wired into `mamba_mixer2` and `qwen_gdn_linear_attn`.
- The `mamba_attn` and `gdn_attn` metadata builders carry the cursors.
- `MambaStateShapeCalculator` sizes the caches.
- The conv path reuses `causal_conv1d_update` unchanged.

**What gets cached per token:**
- **Mamba2:** `x`, `dt` and `B`.
- **GDN:** the corrected update u = β(v − Sk), along with k and g. Caching u instead of v keeps the replay free of the serial dependency on the state.
- The read vectors (C or q) are never cached.

**Storage layout:**
- All caches live inside vLLM's paged state blocks.
- Standard decode uses size-B buffers.
- Spec decode uses a circular ring of next_pow2(B+T) slots, where T = num_spec + 1.
- Dtypes: the checkpoint follows the SSM cache dtype (fp32 by default), the input vectors use the activation dtype, and dt/g are always fp32. A later commit switched the GDN d/k caches to fp16.

**Flushing:**
- In standard decode, a flush happens every B steps.
- In spec decode, a flush happens whenever the history plus T would exceed B.

**How rollback works:**
- Baseline vLLM spec decode stores a state snapshot per draft token.
- ReplaySSM makes rollback a pointer move instead, using two cursors: `post_origin` and `write_pos`.
- On a normal step, a device kernel adds `num_accepted` to `write_pos`, so rejected drafts are simply never committed.
- On a flush, `post_origin` advances and `write_pos` resets.
- These commits run on-device during the next metadata build, so there is no device→host sync.

**Parallel verification:** All T draft outputs are computed in a single GEMM from the checkpoint plus the buffer.

**CUDA graphs:** Every step launches both a verify kernel and a flush kernel. Each row early-exits from the launch that doesn't apply to it, so one captured graph per batch size covers the whole decode path.

## Models evaluated

| Model | SSM type | Precision | Hardware |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3-Nano-4B | Mamba2 | BF16 | H100 |
| Nemotron-3-Super-120B | Mamba2 | NVFP4 | B300, MTP drafter |
| Qwen3.5-4B | GDN | BF16 | H100 |
| Qwen3.5-122B | GDN | NVFP4 | B300, MTP drafter |

- The GDN spec benchmark uses `--spec-method qwen3_next_mtp`.
- Some kernel tests also cover Mamba2-2.7B, Nemotron-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-27B.

## Benchmarks

**Standard decode, end-to-end speedup** (fp32 state, B=16):

| Model | bs1 | bs512 |
|---|---|---|
| Nano-4B | 0.99× | 1.55× |
| Qwen3.5-4B | 0.99× | 1.31× |
| Super-120B | 0.98× | 1.67× |
| Qwen-122B | 0.98× | 1.20× |

- At the kernel level, speedups saturate around 1.4–1.9× by bs128–256.
- At bs1 the kernel can be slower (as low as 0.57×).
- B=16 is the best buffer length; B=32 drops the Super-120B kernel to about 0.85–0.98×.

**Spec decode** (GSM8K, B300, T = 4 or 6, B=16):
- **Versus native spec:** about 1.0–1.1× at bs1, rising to 1.8–2.45× at bs256–512. Qwen-122B at T=6 ran out of memory at bs512.
- **Versus no-spec autoregressive:** about 1.8–2.5× across batch sizes.
- **Acceptance length matches native spec:** for example, Super-120B at T=4 gets 3.56 vs 3.41, and Qwen-122B at T=4 gets 3.56 vs 3.56.
- **B=32 vs B=16:** B=32 is slightly better (e.g., Super-120B T=6 at bs512: 2.49 vs 2.45).
- **Max concurrency** at mml=2048 and (B,T)=(16,4): Super-120B goes from 213 to 694 requests (3.25×), and Qwen-122B from 233 to 702 (3.01×).
- **Verify kernel latency** on Super-120B is about 263–324 µs.

## Limitations and future work

- Only fp32 state has been evaluated. FP16/BF16 state is at roughly baseline parity on B300.
- TP>1 is untested.
- Precision studies are still pending.

## Other topics asked about

- **ROCm/AMD:** not mentioned. Only NVIDIA H100 and B300 are used.
- **Tree drafts:** not mentioned. Spec decode is described only with a linear T-token window and an MTP drafter.

- Only fp32 state has been evaluated. FP16/BF16 state is at roughly baseline parity on B300.

## Other topics asked about

- **ROCm/AMD:** not mentioned. Only NVIDIA H100 and B300 are used.
- **Tree drafts:** not mentioned. Spec decode is described only with a linear T-token window and an MTP drafter.

**Title:** [Feature]: Faster hybrid-SSM decode via input "replay" ring buffer (ReplaySSM), Issue #46187, vllm-project/vllm

**Author:** mgoin
**Status:** Open. Assigned to Johnny-Liou. Labels: *feature request*, *speculative-decoding*.
**Created:** June 19, 2026

**Summary**
- **Problem:** Decode for hybrid models with SSM layers (Mamba2, Gated DeltaNet) is limited by memory bandwidth. Each step loads the recurrent state from HBM, updates it, and stores it again. The state is large, for example Mamba2's `(num_heads, head_dim, d_state)` per layer. The issue says the write-back "dominates at batch-1 decode."
- **Proposal:** ReplaySSM is a research fork based on vLLM commit `193ce8812`. It keeps recent SSM *inputs* in a small ring buffer for each layer and replays them to rebuild state when needed, instead of writing the full state back every step. The trade is a little extra compute for less HBM traffic, which the issue likens to FlashAttention's IO-vs-recompute approach.
- **Claimed benefits:**
  - Lower memory traffic for autoregressive decode at small batch sizes.
  - Cheaper state rollback in speculative decoding. Rejecting draft tokens normally means checkpointing the full state; with the buffer, you just move a cursor and replay.
- **Numbers:** The issue gives no figures. It only says the fork reports end-to-end AR and spec-decode throughput gains on H100/B300 with Nemotron-Nano-4B and Qwen3.5 4B/122B.
- **Integration:** Opt-in Triton kernels would sit next to `selective_state_update` (Mamba2) and `fused_recurrent` (GDN). They would be enabled by the flags `--use-replayssm`, `--use-replayssm-spec`, `--replayssm-buffer-len` and `--replayssm-route`.
- **Open questions:**
  - Numerical parity, since "No parity data in the fork yet."
  - Whether TP1 and TP2 produce matching outputs.
  - Maintenance: the fork duplicates kernels per architecture and should be unified under `ssu_dispatch.py`.
  - How sensitive results are to buffer length, and what a safe default would be.

**Key comments and activity**
- **adityakamat24 (Jun 21):** Offered to take on the work.
- **A1c0r-Z (Jun 22):** Pushed two fork commits that reference the issue: "[Kernel] ReplaySSM opt-in AR decode for Mamba2" (37e72c5) and "ReplaySSM Mamba2 AR-decode E2E wiring" (a084123).
- **Johnny-Liou (Jun 23), ReplaySSM co-author:** Said the summary is accurate. The team is working with NVIDIA collaborators to finalize the kernel and interface design, and they "plan to bring the PR ourselves." mgoin then assigned the issue to him.
- **seanwestfall (Sep 7):** Offered to help with integration, correctness tests or benchmarks inside the existing effort rather than build a competing one.
- **PRs:** None yet. The page says "No branches or pull requests."

**Links**
- Fork: https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM
- Author's X post: https://x.com/zwljohnny/status/2066517132733509756

**PR #49887: "[Kernel] ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs for faster Gated DeltaNet speculative decode"**

- **Author:** Johnny-Liou. It is a collaboration between Dao AI Lab and NVIDIA, and some commits are co-authored by Claude Opus 5.
- **Status:** Open, not merged. It has the "needs-rebase" label because of merge conflicts flagged on Jul 27, 2026. It also carries the performance, qwen and v1 labels.
- **Created:** Jul 26, 2026. Commits were pushed Jul 25, 2026.
- **Merged:** Not merged. No merge date.
- **Stacking:** It sits on top of #49847 (Mamba2 speculative decode), so the diff includes that PR's commits. It is the fourth sub-PR split out of draft #47576.

**Summary of the change**
- Native GDN speculative decode keeps one recurrent state snapshot per draft token. That means T states per step, so the cost grows linearly with T.
- ReplaySSM replaces those snapshots with a single checkpoint and a small circular buffer of per-step inputs `(d, k, g)`. Here `d = beta * (v - S k)` is the delta-rule update.
- With this design:
  - Rolling back rejected drafts only moves a cursor.
  - Every draft output is computed from the same checkpoint.
  - The full state is written out only during a periodic flush.
- **Additions:**
  - A new kernel, `gdn_replayssm_spec_decode`.
  - Cursor helpers `commit_gdn_replayssm_spec` and `reset_gdn_replayssm_spec_cursors`.
  - Blackwell launch configs.
  - Integration with the Qwen3.5 GDN mixer, which now declares `SupportsReplaySSM`.
  - The paged state grows to five tensors: conv, ssm, d_cache, k_cache and g_cache.
- **Precision:** The d and k caches use fp16 when activations are bf16. g is always fp32.
- **Routing:** Every post-prefill row goes through the spec kernel. A row with no drafts runs as a T=1 window.

**Flags and constraints**
- The feature is enabled with `--use-replayssm-spec`, which was introduced in #49847. With the flag off, the decode path is unchanged.
- The validator requires speculative decoding, `mamba_cache_mode none` and the Triton backend.
- It rejects prefix caching, P/D disaggregation and KV connectors, and stochastic rounding.
- Only fp32 state was evaluated. fp16 and bf16 state are handled in code but not evaluated.

**Benchmarks**
Setup: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4 on one B300, TP1, fp32 state, B=16, MTP drafter, GSM8K greedy.

- **Kernel speedup vs the baseline fused kernel:** 1.79x at bs128/T=2, rising to 4.46x at bs512/T=8.
- **End-to-end vs native spec:** roughly 0.87–1.12x at bs1, 1.05–1.22x at bs32, 1.35–1.84x at bs128, 1.36–2.09x at bs256, and 1.73x/2.10x at bs512 (T=2/T=4).
- **The bs512 T=6 and T=8 runs ran out of memory.** The authors attribute this to profiling-time temporary KV allocation, not to ReplaySSM itself.
- **End-to-end vs no-spec decode:** about 1.4–2.1x across batch sizes. At bs512, ReplaySSM reached 19,707 tok/s, versus 10,398 for standard decode and about 9.2–9.4k for native spec.
- **Acceptance length:** essentially the same as native spec (for example 5.53 vs 5.52 at T=8).
- **Serving capacity:** max concurrency is 656.5 vs 233.2, a 2.81x improvement.
- **Accuracy:** within 0.9 points on gsm8k, mmlu_pro, gpqa and hmmt. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on 2xH100 TP2 showed the same parity.
- **Test hardware:** kernel tests ran on an A100 and engine parity on an H100.

**ROCm/AMD:** The page does not discuss it.

**TP support:** Only TP1 (the 122B model) and TP2 (the 35B parity check) are mentioned. There is no other discussion of tensor parallelism.

**Prefix caching**
- It is out of scope for this PR.
- F21HGG proposed an exact-order "recover SSM" path that supports `align` mode and prefix caching. They reported FP16-state divergence from native at token 8 when testing this PR's design.
- hnover-nv (NVIDIA) said align support is being worked on separately. They argued replay should actually be more accurate with fp16 state, since quantization happens only when the buffer flushes.
- askliar said a FlashInfer path is coming that will include prefix caching. F21HGG agreed to use the unified path.
- benchislett said "Prefix caching is a hard requirement" and favored ReplaySSM over RecoverSSM.
- erdholion shared production data: a 49.8% prefix-cache hit rate alongside 2.45 of 3 MTP tokens accepted. They offered to run A/B tests on an RTX 5090.
- Follow-up draft PR #56466 adds prefix caching for GDN speculative decode.

**Reviews**
- The Claude bot's automated review was disabled because the PR comes from a fork.
- About 20 code owners were requested as reviewers, but none have reviewed yet. At least one approval is required to merge.

# ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State

## Date and authors
- **Date:** The page shows no explicit date. The asset paths suggest **2026-06-15**, and the copyright reads 2026.
- **Authors:** No byline appears. The post is on Tri Dao's blog, and the code repo is under the GitHub user "Johnny-Liou." The full author list is not stated.

## Why native vLLM speculative decoding underperforms on hybrid models

**SSM decoding is memory-bound.**
- Each step loads and stores an FP32 state of shape (nheads, d, n).
- Arithmetic intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte, versus roughly 300 for an H100 matmul.
- Baseline traffic per head is 8dn + 2(d+2n+1), dominated by the 8dn state term.
- On Nemotron-3-Super (batch 256, B300), the SSM kernel is the largest latency component up to 100K tokens.
- SSM layers outnumber attention layers 3:1 to 5:1 in these models.

**Per-draft state snapshots.**
- vLLM keeps a separate SSM state for each speculative token so it can roll back on rejection.
- This adds "T times more memory traffic per decoding step" (T = speculative window).
- At T=6, the baseline kernel costs **4.85×** the standard decode kernel (Qwen3.5-122B, batch 128).

**Sequential kernel.**
- Verification is a serial length-T recurrence loop, not a batched GEMM.
- Every intermediate state must be computed and stored.

**HBM footprint.**
- With T=4, the preallocated snapshots cut the maximum decode batch by roughly **4×** compared with standard serving.

## The ReplaySSM algorithm

**Core idea.** Keep a checkpoint state S₀ plus a small buffer of recent inputs (v, Δ, k) instead of writing the state back every step.

**Output-only decode (Mamba-2).**
- The output is computed directly: y = ā(S₀q) + Σ s_j (k_jᵀq) v_j.
- No d×n state is materialized.
- A small precompute kernel computes the shared k_jᵀq once per head group.
- Per-step traffic becomes 4dn + buffer terms, roughly halving the dominant state traffic.
- Results match the baseline up to floating-point error.

**Flush.**
- When the buffer is full, the cached inputs are folded into S₀ and the full state is written back once.
- For speculative decoding, the flush fires when h + 2T > L (one window early), so a full draft window is always available.
- Only committed inputs are flushed; the current step's drafts are not.

**Parallel verification of T drafts.**
- All drafts read the same checkpoint and buffer.
- M = KᵀQ is computed as a GEMM with a causal mask.
- The weighted sum over v is a second GEMM.

**Rollback.**
- Rollback is just a pointer move in a ring buffer, which avoids data-dependent copies.
- A device-side commit kernel advances the pointers, avoiding host synchronization.
- The per-sequence flush decision is read at runtime, so the path works under CUDA Graph.

**GDN-specific trick.**
- ReplaySSM caches u = β(v − Sk) instead of raw v. The update then becomes S_t = α_t S_{t−1} + u_t k_tᵀ, which unrolls like Mamba-2.
- Standard GDN decoding uses the state-and-output route, because both Sk and Sq are needed.
- For speculative decoding, it applies GDN's chunk-wise training approach:
  - A_{s,s'} = β_s e^{G_s−G_{s'}}(k_s·k_{s'}) is strictly lower triangular.
  - W = (I+A)⁻¹ requires one T×T triangular solve.
  - Everything else is GEMMs.
- No WY form is named explicitly.

## Benchmark setup and results

**Models and hardware:**

| Model | Precision | GPUs |
|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3-Nano-4B | BF16 | 1×H100 |
| Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B | NVFP4 | 1×B300 |
| Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B | NVFP4 | 2×B300, TP2 |
| Qwen3.5-4B | BF16 | 1×H100 |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | NVFP4 | 1×B300 |

- Implemented in vLLM with CUDA Graph enabled.
- FP32 state, BF16 buffer.
- MTP heads serve as drafters.

**Standard decoding** (batch 256, 1K steps; buffer 8 for Nemotron, 16 for Qwen):

| Family | Kernel speedup | End-to-end speedup |
|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3 | 1.43–1.84× | 1.20–1.48× |
| Qwen3.5 | 1.43–1.64× | 1.20–1.27× |

- Large MoE models reach up to 1.43× end-to-end.
- A buffer sweep (sizes 4/8/16/32 at batch 64 and 256) shows a bell-shaped curve.

**Speculative decoding** (GSM8K, T=4, temperature 0, batch up to 512):
- **1.87–1.96×** over standard decoding.
- Up to **2.14×** over vLLM's speculative baseline; the gap widens with batch size.
- Acceptance is identical across systems.
- At T=6, ReplaySSM's kernel cost is 1.27–1.72× of standard decoding, versus 4.85× for the baseline.
- At T=4, the speedup over the speculative baseline narrows across levels:
  - kernel: 2.28–3.33×
  - verify pass: 1.23–1.69×
  - full step: 1.20–1.58×
- Maximum concurrency is **3.0–3.3×** higher.

## Tree-based speculative decoding
The ring buffer with in-kernel indexing is described as important for tree-based speculation, where accepted tokens are not contiguous. No tree-based results are reported.

## AMD/ROCm
Not mentioned. All results are on NVIDIA H100 and B300.

## Limitations and caveats
- End-to-end gains are smaller than kernel gains because only the SSM kernel changes.
- Larger buffers increase reads and can make the kernel compute-bound. Speculative decoding also causes more frequent flushes.
- Whether the FLOP reduction speeds up compute-bound cases is unclear, since the outer-product route can use Tensor Cores. This "requires deeper exploration."
- The GDN path cannot use the shared k·q precompute.
- Mamba-3 and GDN2 support is left for future work.
- Prior methods (Mamba-in-the-Llama, STree) still write the state every step and were evaluated only on Mamba-2 at batch size 1.

- The per-sequence flush decision is read at runtime, so the path works under CUDA Graph.

**GDN-specific trick.**
- ReplaySSM caches u = β(v − Sk) instead of raw v. The update then becomes S_t = α_t S_{t−1} + u_t k_tᵀ, which unrolls like Mamba-2.
- Standard GDN decoding uses the state-and-output route, because both Sk and Sq are needed.
- For speculative decoding, it applies GDN's chunk-wise training approach:
  - A_{s,s'} = β_s e^{G_s−G_{s'}}(k_s·k_{s'}) is strictly lower triangular.
  - W = (I+A)⁻¹ requires one T×T triangular solve.
  - Everything else is GEMMs.
- No WY form is named explicitly.

## Benchmark setup and results

**Models and hardware:**

| Model | Precision | GPUs |
|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3-Nano-4B | BF16 | 1×H100 |
| Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B | NVFP4 | 1×B300 |
| Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B | NVFP4 | 2×B300, TP2 |
| Qwen3.5-4B | BF16 | 1×H100 |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | NVFP4 | 1×B300 |

- Implemented in vLLM with CUDA Graph enabled.
- FP32 state, BF16 buffer.
- MTP heads serve as drafters.

**Standard decoding** (batch 256, 1K steps; buffer 8 for Nemotron, 16 for Qwen):

| Family | Kernel speedup | End-to-end speedup |
|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3 | 1.43–1.84× | 1.20–1.48× |
| Qwen3.5 | 1.43–1.64× | 1.20–1.27× |

- Large MoE models reach up to 1.43× end-to-end.
- A buffer sweep (sizes 4/8/16/32 at batch 64 and 256) shows a bell-shaped curve.

**Speculative decoding** (GSM8K, T=4, temperature 0, batch up to 512):
- **1.87–1.96×** over standard decoding.
- Up to **2.14×** over vLLM's speculative baseline; the gap widens with batch size.
- Acceptance is identical across systems.
- At T=6, ReplaySSM's kernel cost is 1.27–1.72× of standard decoding, versus 4.85× for the baseline.
- At T=4, the speedup over the speculative baseline narrows across levels:
  - kernel: 2.28–3.33×
  - verify pass: 1.23–1.69×
  - full step: 1.20–1.58×
- Maximum concurrency is **3.0–3.3×** higher.

## Tree-based speculative decoding
The ring buffer with in-kernel indexing is described as important for tree-based speculation, where accepted tokens are not contiguous. No tree-based results are reported.

## AMD/ROCm
Not mentioned. All results are on NVIDIA H100 and B300.

## Limitations and caveats
- End-to-end gains are smaller than kernel gains because only the SSM kernel changes.
- Larger buffers increase reads and can make the kernel compute-bound. Speculative decoding also causes more frequent flushes.
- Whether the FLOP reduction speeds up compute-bound cases is unclear, since the outer-product route can use Tensor Cores. This "requires deeper exploration."
- The GDN path cannot use the shared k·q precompute.
- Mamba-3 and GDN2 support is left for future work.
- Prior methods (Mamba-in-the-Llama, STree) still write the state every step and were evaluated only on Mamba-2 at batch size 1.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MambaSpec(KVCacheSpec):
    shapes: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]
    dtypes: tuple[torch.dtype, ...]
    page_size_padded: int | None = None
    mamba_type: MambaAttentionBackendEnum = MambaAttentionBackendEnum.MAMBA2
    mamba_cache_mode: str = "none"
    num_speculative_blocks: int = 0
    num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks: int = 0
    prefill_checkpoint_alignment: int | None = None
    num_heads: int = 1
    tokens_per_state: int = -1
    # False: the state is sharded across TP ranks (e.g. GDN). True: every TP
    # rank holds the full state (e.g. the replicated PLE conv state).
    tp_replicated: bool = False

    @property
    def state_content_size_bytes(self) -> int:
        return sum(
            prod(shape) * get_dtype_size(dtype)
            for (shape, dtype) in zip(self.shapes, self.dtypes)
        )

    @property
    def real_page_size_bytes(self) -> int:
        return self.state_content_size_bytes

    @property
    def page_size_bytes(self) -> int:
        page_size = sum(
            prod(shape) * get_dtype_size(dtype)
            for (shape, dtype) in zip(self.shapes, self.dtypes)
        )
        if self.page_size_padded is not None:
            assert self.page_size_padded >= page_size
            return self.page_size_padded
        return page_size

    @property
    def block_table_token_alignment(self) -> int | None:
        return None

    def max_memory_usage_bytes(self, vllm_config: VllmConfig) -> int:
        if vllm_config.cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "align":
            return self.page_size_bytes * (
                2 + self.num_speculative_blocks + self.num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks
            )
        else:
            return self.page_size_bytes * (1 + self.num_speculative_blocks)

    def max_num_blocks_per_req(self, vllm_config: VllmConfig, max_len: int) -> int:
        # Mamba state is replicated across DCP/PCP ranks, never sharded, so
        # no CP scaling applies.
        if vllm_config.cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "align":
            # Block table rows are position-indexed over the full sequence
            # even though only 2 + num_speculative_blocks state blocks are
            # resident at a time (earlier states are nulled out by
            # remove_skipped_blocks), so the row length must cover max_len
            # rather than max_memory_usage_bytes.
            return cdiv(max_len, self.block_size) + self.num_speculative_blocks
        return cdiv(self.max_memory_usage_bytes(vllm_config), self.page_size_bytes)

    def is_uniform_with_collection(
        self, kv_cache_specs: dict[str, KVCacheSpec]
    ) -> bool:
        return all(
            isinstance(spec, MambaSpec)
            and spec.num_speculative_blocks == self.num_speculative_blocks
            and spec.num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks == self.num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks
            and spec.prefill_checkpoint_alignment == self.prefill_checkpoint_alignment
            and spec.page_size_bytes == self.page_size_bytes
            and spec.tp_replicated == self.tp_replicated
            for spec in kv_cache_specs.values()
        )

    (when not-None) ignores gpu_memory_utilization"""

    kv_offloading_size: float | None = None
    """Size of the KV cache offloading buffer in GiB. When TP > 1, this is
    the total buffer size summed across all TP ranks. By default, this is set
    to None, which means no KV offloading is enabled. When set, vLLM will
----------
    @property
    def prefix_cacheable(self) -> bool:
        return False

    @property
    def uses_slot_mapping(self) -> bool:
        return False


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MambaSpec(KVCacheSpec):
    shapes: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]
    dtypes: tuple[torch.dtype, ...]
    page_size_padded: int | None = None
    mamba_type: MambaAttentionBackendEnum = MambaAttentionBackendEnum.MAMBA2
    mamba_cache_mode: str = "none"
    num_speculative_blocks: int = 0
    num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks: int = 0
    prefill_checkpoint_alignment: int | None = None
    num_heads: int = 1
    tokens_per_state: int = -1
    # False: the state is sharded across TP ranks (e.g. GDN). True: every TP
    # rank holds the full state (e.g. the replicated PLE conv state).
    tp_replicated: bool = False

    @property
    def state_content_size_bytes(self) -> int:
        return sum(
            prod(shape) * get_dtype_size(dtype)
            for (shape, dtype) in zip(self.shapes, self.dtypes)
        )

    @property
    def real_page_size_bytes(self) -> int:
        return self.state_content_size_bytes

    @property
    def page_size_bytes(self) -> int:
        page_size = sum(
            prod(shape) * get_dtype_size(dtype)
            for (shape, dtype) in zip(self.shapes, self.dtypes)
        )
        if self.page_size_padded is not None:
            assert self.page_size_padded >= page_size
            return self.page_size_padded
        return page_size

    @property
    def block_table_token_alignment(self) -> int | None:
        return None

    def max_memory_usage_bytes(self, vllm_config: VllmConfig) -> int:
        if vllm_config.cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "align":
            return self.page_size_bytes * (
                2 + self.num_speculative_blocks + self.num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks
            )
        else:
            return self.page_size_bytes * (1 + self.num_speculative_blocks)

    def max_num_blocks_per_req(self, vllm_config: VllmConfig, max_len: int) -> int:
        # Mamba state is replicated across DCP/PCP ranks, never sharded, so
        # no CP scaling applies.
        if vllm_config.cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "align":
            # Block table rows are position-indexed over the full sequence
            # even though only 2 + num_speculative_blocks state blocks are
            # resident at a time (earlier states are nulled out by
            # remove_skipped_blocks), so the row length must cover max_len
            # rather than max_memory_usage_bytes.
            return cdiv(max_len, self.block_size) + self.num_speculative_blocks
        return cdiv(self.max_memory_usage_bytes(vllm_config), self.page_size_bytes)

    def is_uniform_with_collection(
        self, kv_cache_specs: dict[str, KVCacheSpec]
    ) -> bool:
        return all(
            isinstance(spec, MambaSpec)
            and spec.num_speculative_blocks == self.num_speculative_blocks
            and spec.num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks == self.num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks
            and spec.prefill_checkpoint_alignment == self.prefill_checkpoint_alignment
            and spec.page_size_bytes == self.page_size_bytes
            and spec.tp_replicated == self.tp_replicated
            for spec in kv_cache_specs.values()
        )
