def _forward_core_rocm(
        self,
        qkvz: torch.Tensor,
        ba: torch.Tensor,
        z_out: torch.Tensor,
        core_attn_out: torch.Tensor,
    ):
        """ROCm AITER fast path: conv1d + recurrent attention from packed
        qkvz/ba layout.

        For decode-only (no spec, no prefill) batches, dispatches directly to
        ``_forward_core_decode_aiter``. Otherwise unpacks the packed layout and
        falls through to ``_forward_core``.

        Args:
            qkvz: packed [q, k, v, z] projection (num_tokens, qkvz_dim)
            ba:   packed [b, a] gating vectors    (num_tokens, 2*num_heads)
            z_out: **output** buffer for z        (num_tokens, num_heads,
                   head_dim); mutated in-place.
            core_attn_out: Pre-allocated output buffer for attention results.

        """
        forward_context = get_forward_context()
        attn_metadata_raw = forward_context.attn_metadata

        attn_metadata = None
        if isinstance(attn_metadata_raw, dict):
            attn_metadata = attn_metadata_raw.get(self.prefix)
        if attn_metadata is None:
            v_dim = core_attn_out.shape[-1] * core_attn_out.shape[-2]
            self._warmup_prefill_kernels(qkvz, v_dim)
            return

        assert isinstance(attn_metadata, GDNAttentionMetadata)

        if (
            attn_metadata.spec_sequence_masks is None
            and attn_metadata.num_prefills == 0
            and attn_metadata.num_decodes > 0
        ):
            return self._forward_core_decode_aiter(
                qkvz=qkvz,
                ba=ba,
                z_out=z_out,
                core_attn_out=core_attn_out,
                attn_metadata=attn_metadata,
            )

        core_attn_out.zero_()
        num_tokens_all = qkvz.shape[0]
        mixed_qkv, z, b, a = self.prepare_gdn_attention_core_inputs(
            qkvz, ba, num_tokens_all
        )
        z_out[:] = z
        self._forward_core(
            mixed_qkv=mixed_qkv,
            b=b,
            a=a,
            core_attn_out=core_attn_out,
        )

    def _forward_core(
.....
        num_accepted_tokens = attn_metadata.num_accepted_tokens

        mixed_qkv = mixed_qkv[:num_actual_tokens]
        b = b[:num_actual_tokens]
        a = a[:num_actual_tokens]

        # 1. Convolution sequence transformation
        conv_weights = self.conv1d.weight.view(
            self.conv1d.weight.size(0), self.conv1d.weight.size(2)
        )

        if spec_sequence_masks is not None:
            if attn_metadata.num_prefills == 0 and attn_metadata.num_decodes == 0:
                mixed_qkv_spec = mixed_qkv
                a_spec = a
                b_spec = b
                mixed_qkv_non_spec = None
            else:
                mixed_qkv_spec = mixed_qkv.index_select(0, spec_token_indx)
                a_spec = a.index_select(0, spec_token_indx)
                b_spec = b.index_select(0, spec_token_indx)
                mixed_qkv_non_spec = mixed_qkv.index_select(0, non_spec_token_indx)
        else:
            mixed_qkv_spec = None
            mixed_qkv_non_spec = mixed_qkv

        # 1.1: Process the multi-query part
        if spec_sequence_masks is not None:
            # spec_state_indices_tensor is always set when spec_sequence_masks is set
            assert spec_state_indices_tensor is not None
            mixed_qkv_spec = causal_conv1d_update(
                mixed_qkv_spec,
                conv_state,
                conv_weights,
                self.conv1d.bias,
                self.activation,
                conv_state_indices=spec_state_indices_tensor[:, 0][  # type: ignore[index]
                    : attn_metadata.num_spec_decodes  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
                ],
                num_accepted_tokens=num_accepted_tokens,
                query_start_loc=spec_query_start_loc,
                max_query_len=spec_state_indices_tensor.size(-1),
                validate_data=False,
            )

        # 1.2: Process the remaining part
        if attn_metadata.num_prefills > 0:
            assert mixed_qkv_non_spec is not None
            mixed_qkv_non_spec_T = mixed_qkv_non_spec.transpose(0, 1)
            # - "cache_indices" updates the conv_state cache in positions
            #   pointed to by "state_indices_tensor"
            mixed_qkv_non_spec = causal_conv1d_fn(
                mixed_qkv_non_spec_T,
                conv_weights,
                self.conv1d.bias,
                activation=self.activation,
                conv_states=conv_state,
                has_initial_state=has_initial_state,
                cache_indices=non_spec_state_indices_tensor,
                query_start_loc=non_spec_query_start_loc,
                metadata=attn_metadata,
            ).transpose(0, 1)
        elif attn_metadata.num_decodes > 0:
            assert mixed_qkv_non_spec is not None
            mixed_qkv_non_spec = causal_conv1d_update(
                mixed_qkv_non_spec,
                conv_state,
                conv_weights,
                self.conv1d.bias,
                self.activation,
                conv_state_indices=non_spec_state_indices_tensor[  # type: ignore[index]
                    : attn_metadata.num_actual_tokens  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
                ],
                validate_data=True,
            )
        else:
            mixed_qkv_non_spec = None

        split_non_spec = (
            spec_sequence_masks is None
            and attn_metadata.num_prefills > 0
            and attn_metadata.num_decodes > 0
        )
        num_decode_tokens = attn_metadata.num_decode_tokens

        if attn_metadata.num_prefills > 0:
            assert mixed_qkv_non_spec is not None, (
                "mixed_qkv_non_spec must be provided for prefill path"
            )
            if spec_sequence_masks is not None:
                a_non_spec = a.index_select(0, non_spec_token_indx)
                b_non_spec = b.index_select(0, non_spec_token_indx)
            else:
                a_non_spec = a
                b_non_spec = b

            if split_non_spec:
                conv_output_prefill = mixed_qkv_non_spec[num_decode_tokens:]
                a_prefill = a_non_spec[num_decode_tokens:]
                b_prefill = b_non_spec[num_decode_tokens:]
            else:
                conv_output_prefill = mixed_qkv_non_spec
                a_prefill = a_non_spec
                b_prefill = b_non_spec

            (
                query_non_spec,
                key_non_spec,
                value_non_spec,
                g_non_spec,
                beta_non_spec,
            ) = fused_post_conv_prep(
                conv_output=conv_output_prefill,
                a=a_prefill,
                b=b_prefill,
                A_log=self.A_log,
                dt_bias=self.dt_bias,
                num_k_heads=self.num_k_heads // self.tp_size,
                head_k_dim=self.head_k_dim,
                head_v_dim=self.head_v_dim,
                apply_l2norm=True,
                output_g_exp=False,
            )
            query_non_spec = query_non_spec.unsqueeze(0)
            key_non_spec = key_non_spec.unsqueeze(0)
            value_non_spec = value_non_spec.unsqueeze(0)
            g_non_spec = g_non_spec.unsqueeze(0)
            beta_non_spec = beta_non_spec.unsqueeze(0)
        else:
            query_non_spec, key_non_spec, value_non_spec = self.rearrange_mixed_qkv(
                mixed_qkv_non_spec
            )
            g_non_spec = None
            beta_non_spec = None

        # 2. Recurrent attention

        # 2.1: Process the multi-query part
        if spec_sequence_masks is not None:
            core_attn_out_spec, last_recurrent_state = (
                fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update(
                    A_log=self.A_log,
                    a=a_spec,
                    b=b_spec,
                    dt_bias=self.dt_bias,
                    q=query_spec,
                    k=key_spec,
                    v=value_spec,
                    initial_state=ssm_state,
                    inplace_final_state=True,
                    cu_seqlens=spec_query_start_loc[  # type: ignore[index]
                        : attn_metadata.num_spec_decodes
                        + 1  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
                    ],
                    ssm_state_indices=spec_state_indices_tensor,
                    num_accepted_tokens=num_accepted_tokens,
                    use_qk_l2norm_in_kernel=True,
                )

import sys, json, urllib.request, urllib.parse, time, re
q = sys.argv[1]; pages = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 1
filt = re.compile(sys.argv[3], re.I) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else None
order = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else "asc"
for p in range(1, pages + 1):
    url = "https://api.github.com/search/issues?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({"q": q, "per_page": 100, "page": p, "sort": "created", "order": order})
    try:
        d = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60))
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERR", e); break
    if p == 1: print("## %s total=%s" % (q, d.get("total_count")))
    items = d.get("items", [])
    for it in items:
        pr = "PR" if "pull_request" in it else "IS"
        merged = (it.get("pull_request") or {}).get("merged_at")
        t = it["title"]
        if filt and not filt.search(t): continue
        print(pr, "#%d" % it["number"], it["created_at"][:10], it["state"], ("merged=" + str(merged)[:10]) if pr == "PR" else "", "|", t[:150], "|", it["user"]["login"])
    if len(items) < 100: break
    time.sleep(7)
EOF

**Issue #39273 (vllm-project/vllm): "[Bug]: Ngram speculative decoding produces corrupted output on hybrid GDN (Qwen3.5) models"**

- **Author:** bhaktatejas922
- **Opened:** April 8, 2026
- **Status:** Open. It is assigned to tdoublep and tracked in the "Qwen3.5+" project with status "In progress."

**Reported symptom**
- **Original report:**
  - Model: Qwen3.5-9B with FP8 (compressed-tensors) and the `qwen3_5_text` architecture, which has 24 GatedDeltaNet layers and 8 full-attention layers.
  - vLLM version: `0.18.1rc1.dev43`, also reproduced on nightly `dev236`.
  - Hardware: GH200.
  - Settings: `--enforce-eager`, chunked prefill, Triton GDN prefill backend, and ngram with `num_speculative_tokens: 64` and `prompt_lookup_min/max 2/10`.
  - Result: at temperature 0, output fills with repeated or truncated fragments. There is no crash or error.
- **Configurations the author tested:**
  - ngram with prefix caching off (`mamba_cache_mode=none`): corrupted.
  - ngram with prefix caching on (`align`): corrupted.
  - suffix with prefix caching off: corrupted.
- **Other reports:**
  - **Eagle3:** the author says it worked fine.
  - **Mamba2 hybrid (swesty):** on `nemotron_h` (Nemotron-3-Nano-30B NVFP4, v0.22.1rc1, GB10), ngram and ngram_gpu went 0/20 on correctness while acceptance stayed at 64–81%. The #40875 workaround (`prompt_lookup_min=8`) did not help.
  - **Qwen3.8-27B with MTP (ch2lab):** shows the same corruption class.
  - **Qwen3.8-27B on RTX 5090 (hifiberry):** v0.26.1rc1 with ngram k=3 corrupted tool-call arguments. The corruption was deterministic within one engine instance but did not recur after a restart.

**Diagnosed root cause (evolving, community analysis only)**
1. **Initial theory.** `postprocess_mamba` in `mamba_utils.py` can't roll back GDN SSM state that had already advanced through all N proposed tokens.
2. **Revised theory.** The fused_recurrent kernel already selects its starting state using `num_accepted_tokens`. The author then suspected too few `ssm_state_indices` slots for speculative tokens, so writes for rejected tokens overwrite accepted state.
3. **ch2lab's later diagnosis.** In `align` mode, `preprocess_mamba` moves the state forward to the next block. When `new_num_computed` lands on a block boundary, `postprocess_mamba_fused_kernel` can then copy backward (`src_block_idx > dest_block_idx`), overwriting the migrated state.
   - Proposed fix: skip that case in both `postprocess_mamba_fused_kernel` and `collect_mamba_copy_meta`.
   - ch2lab argues this path is shared by every proposer. hifiberry's own arithmetic reproduces the pattern: 0 forward copies and 60 backward copies in their sweep.

The page does not discuss rows with zero or variable draft tokens going through a non-spec path, or conv-state rollback specifically.

**Suffix decoding**
The author states that "any prompt-matching spec dec method (ngram, suffix) corrupts GDN SSM state on token rejection." Suffix is confirmed corrupted in the test table.

**Linked PRs and commits**
- **PR #40738:** shown as linked and open. Its content isn't on the page.
- **Fork commits referencing the issue:**
  - AjAnubolu: "[Bugfix] Fix ngram spec decode corrupted output…"
  - ch2lab: "guard backward mamba state copy in fused postprocess"
  - hav4ik: documentation commits
- **#40875:** a related config-only workaround issue.

**Maintainer comments**
- benchislett: "Will need to take a deeper look," then CC'd tdoublep.
- vadiklyutiy: asked the author to try MTP and to confirm that Eagle behaves correctly.
- No maintainer has proposed a fix or named a vLLM version that resolves the bug.
- hifiberry asked ch2lab for the trigger-enumeration script so the guard can be A/B tested; that request is still open.

## PR #40738: "[Bugfix] Fix GDN conv + SSM state corruption with ngram spec decode"

- **Author:** tdoublep (Thomas Parnell, IBM). The commit is co-authored with Claude Opus 4.6, and the PR is disclosed as AI-assisted.
- **Dates:** Opened Apr 23, 2026. Force-pushed and marked ready for review Apr 24, 2026. Last activity on the page is Sep 6, 2026.
- **Status:** Still **open** and unmerged. Labels are `bug`, `v1`, `needs-rebase` and `unstale`. Mergify flagged merge conflicts on May 23 and again on Sep 6. It was marked stale on Aug 24, then unstaled after a new comment.
- **Original title:** "Fix GDN SSM state corruption with ngram speculative decoding." The author later added "conv" to the title.

### The bug
Hybrid GDN models such as Qwen3.5 produce corrupted output when ngram speculative decoding runs with `mamba_cache_mode="none"`.

### Root cause
After a spec step accepts N tokens, the next regular decode step needs SSM state from block N-1 and conv state from an offset position. Instead it read from block 0. Two gaps caused this:
1. `num_accepted_tokens` was not passed to the SSM metadata builders on non-spec steps.
2. `causal_conv1d_fn` had no way to offset its conv-state reads by the number of accepted tokens.

### Fix approach
- **`gdn_attn.py`:** computes `spec_decode_src_indices`. In mixed batches, it pads `num_accepted_tokens` with 1s for prefill sequences.
- **`gdn_linear_attn.py`:** copies SSM state from the accepted block into block 0 ahead of time. It passes `num_accepted_tokens` to the conv kernels only when a correction is needed.
- **`causal_conv1d.py`:** adds an `IS_SPEC_DECODING` path to `_causal_conv1d_fwd_kernel` that offsets conv-state reads and writes by `num_accepted_tokens - 1`.
- **`gpu_model_runner.py`:** passes `num_accepted_tokens` to the GDN and Mamba2 builders on non-spec steps.
- **Testing:** token-for-token match against baseline on Qwen3.5-0.8B, plus mixed-batch checks.

### Linked issues and references
- **Fixes:** #39273, the original report by bhaktatejas922.
- **Referenced by:**
  - #40831 (TurboQuant with spec decode)
  - #40875 (ngram `prompt_lookup_min`)
  - #40880 (MTP/TurboQuant)
  - #36138
  - #50226
  - #53229
  - #55504

### Review and discussion
- **gemini-code-assist:** warned that in mixed batches, decode requests might read stale SSM state because the code defaults to the first block when prefills are present. The thread is shown as resolved.
- **claude[bot]:** automated review was disabled because the PR comes from a fork.
- **Requested code-owner reviewers:** njhill, ZJY0516, vadiklyutiy and tomeras91. None of them has approved yet.
- **Sandermage:** backported the fix to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 and saw tool-call clean rates rise from about 20% to 53–70%.
  - They pointed out that the decode-only `_causal_conv1d_update_kernel` already had `IS_SPEC_DECODING`, so the real gap was the asymmetry with the fwd kernel.
  - Reaching 100% also required `prompt_lookup_min=8`, which addresses a separate ngram issue.
- **bhaktatejas922:** reported that it works at batch size 1 but breaks above that. Their follow-up commit 04e09d5 explains that the PR only fixes the case where every request in the batch is non-spec, not the mixed-batch branch.
  - In that branch the code still reads "block_table[~mask, 0]" and drops the non-spec accepted counts.
  - Their fix brought BS=8 accuracy from 0.57 back to about 0.957, roughly parity with BS=1.
- **DimensionSTP (Sep 3, 2026):** confirmed the mixed-batch gap still exists on current main, where the code reads block 10 instead of block 12. They offered to rebase and merge in the follow-up, or to open a superseding PR that keeps attribution to both contributors.

### Suffix decoding and other model-free proposers
The page does not mention suffix decoding. The only model-free proposer discussed is ngram, and MTP comes up only through linked issues.

### Superseded?
The page does not show this PR being superseded. A superseding PR has only been proposed, by DimensionSTP. Their #55504, "Bound GDN speculative decode query widths," mentions this PR, but the page does not describe it as a replacement.

## PR #56531 summary (vllm-project/vllm)

**Title:** "[Bugfix] Route every speculation-capable row through the speculative path so recurrent state stays consistent"

**Author:** vadiklyutiy (Vadim Gimpelson). The commits are co-authored by Cursor Agent, and the description discloses that AI assistance was used.

**Dates:** Opened Sep 11, 2026. Merged Oct 5, 2026 as commit `0eac152`, with 4 commits.

**Closes:** Issue #40875. It cites no other closed issues.

### The bug
- ngram speculative decoding silently corrupts output from hybrid recurrent models. The affected families are Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5 GDN, Nemotron Mamba2 and Kimi-Linear KDA.
- **Trigger:** a step that accepted draft tokens, followed directly by a step that proposed zero drafts.
- **Proposers:**
  - ngram hits this routinely, whenever its lookup finds no match.
  - EAGLE and MTP are said never to trigger it, because they always draft.
  - The suffix proposer isn't discussed in the bug analysis. It only shows up as a CI step name (`spec-decode-ngram-suffix`).
- **Symptoms:** intermittent, workload-dependent dropped or duplicated tokens rather than crashes.

### Root cause
The two decode paths store recurrent state in different places:
- **Non-speculative path:** reads one slot per request, `block_table[:, 0]`.
- **Speculative path:** keeps a window of `num_spec + 1` slots and selects one by `num_accepted_tokens - 1`.

The layouts only agree while one token is accepted. If a row switches paths mid-generation after accepting drafts, it reads a stale slot 0. The read is in bounds, so nothing flags it. The author describes it as "a path switch mid-generation," not a bad index or a race.

### The fix (option 3 of three considered)
Any row that can speculate always takes the speculative path. Zero drafts are treated as `num_spec = 0`.

- **`gdn_attn.py`:** removes the batch-level fallback to the non-speculative path.
- **`gpu_model_runner.py`:**
  - `use_spec_decode` now follows the speculative config instead of the drafts scheduled this step. This is what fixes Mamba2.
  - Zero-draft decode rows are marked `0` instead of `-1`.
  - Chunked-prefill tails are excluded.
  - `num_accepted_tokens` now starts at `1`, which avoids a slot index of `-1` in dummy/profiling runs.
- **`mamba_hybrid.py`:** applies the same fix to the V2 runner, inlined after review.
- **Later commit:** also routes zero-draft KDA rows through the speculative path.

**Validation results (base → patched):**
| Model | Backend | Base | Patched |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 | GDN | 0/60 | 60/60 |
| Nemotron-3-Nano | Mamba2 | 12/60 | 60/60 |
| Kimi-Linear | GDN + KDA | 4/40 | 40/40 |

### Performance implications
- No benchmarks are reported.
- The author argues option 3 needs "No kernel changes, no state copies, no new synchronization." It is described as a classification-only change.
- Rejected alternatives and their costs:
  - **Option 2 (state copy, as in #52942):** a state-sized copy on the step that is meant to stay cheap. It also needs a GPU-resident mirror of acceptance counts under async scheduling.
  - **Option 1 (kernel changes):** would add speculative metadata to the plain decode path.
- The trade-off is that zero-draft rows now go through the speculative path. Its per-step overhead isn't quantified.
- Reviewer benchislett called state-layout changes or extra copy work "a terrible solution that we should avoid." He also noted the issue is "not a burning issue" for DSpark adaptive-verification deployments.

### ROCm/AMD discussion
- DimensionSTP (author of the competing PR #55504) mentioned that #55504 had addressed a ROCm dispatch review.
- He relayed a report from okorzh-amd of an AMD profiling failure:
  - Oversized dummy rows (for example, two 12-token rows with k=7) could pass the decode predicate.
  - Those rows are wider than the `num_speculative_tokens + 1` state-index columns.
- He proposed an inclusive query-length bound, kept in #55504. He had not rerun the AMD failure himself.
- DimensionSTP also said V2 and AMD hardware were not validated in his comparisons.

### Other discussion
- DimensionSTP asked for coordination with #55504, which later adopted this PR's V2 approach with credit. He also contributed CUDA numerical regression tests showing the fix holds at the state level.
- Approved by ZJY0516.

from typing import Any

import torch

from vllm.triton_utils import tl, triton
from vllm.v1.attention.backends.recoverssm_metadata import RecoverSSMMetadata
from vllm.v1.worker.utils import AttentionGroup


class RecoverSSMState:
    """Coordinates RecoverSSM metadata between attention and postprocessing."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._step: tuple[RecoverSSMMetadata, ...] | None = None

    def record_step(
        self,
        attn_metadata: dict[str, Any],
        attn_groups: list[list[AttentionGroup]],
        *,
        for_capture: bool,
    ) -> None:
        if for_capture:
            self._step = None
            return

        step: list[RecoverSSMMetadata] = []
        for group_list in attn_groups:
            for group in group_list:
                metadata = attn_metadata[group.layer_names[0]]
                if isinstance(metadata, RecoverSSMMetadata):
                    step.append(metadata)
        self._step = tuple(step)

    def commit_step(
        self,
        num_sampled: torch.Tensor | int,
        idx_mapping: torch.Tensor,
        *,
        state_indices: torch.Tensor | None,
        num_accepted_tokens: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> None:
        step = self._step
        self._step = None
        if isinstance(num_sampled, int) or step is None:
            return

        for metadata in step:
            postprocess_meta = metadata.commit_recoverssm_state(num_sampled)
            if postprocess_meta is None:
                continue
            assert state_indices is not None
            # RecoverSSM already restored the accepted state. Update its running
            # column and reset the next-step copy bias to the neutral value.
            _postprocess_recoverssm_align_kernel[(postprocess_meta.num_spec_decodes,)](
                idx_mapping,
                num_sampled,
                postprocess_meta.request_indices,
                postprocess_meta.num_computed_tokens,
                state_indices,
                num_accepted_tokens,
                MAMBA_BLOCK_SIZE=postprocess_meta.block_size,
                BLOCK_TABLE_WIDTH=postprocess_meta.block_table.shape[1],
            )


@triton.heuristics(
    {"HAS_REQUEST_INDICES": lambda args: args["request_indices_ptr"] is not None}
)
@triton.jit

class RecoverSSMState:
    """Coordinates RecoverSSM metadata between attention and postprocessing."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._step: tuple[RecoverSSMMetadata, ...] | None = None

    def record_step(
        self,
        attn_metadata: dict[str, Any],
        attn_groups: list[list[AttentionGroup]],
        *,
        for_capture: bool,
    ) -> None:
        if for_capture:
            self._step = None
            return

        step: list[RecoverSSMMetadata] = []
        for group_list in attn_groups:
            for group in group_list:
                metadata = attn_metadata[group.layer_names[0]]
                if isinstance(metadata, RecoverSSMMetadata):
                    step.append(metadata)
        self._step = tuple(step)

    def commit_step(
        self,
        num_sampled: torch.Tensor | int,
        idx_mapping: torch.Tensor,
        *,
        state_indices: torch.Tensor | None,
        num_accepted_tokens: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> None:
        step = self._step
        self._step = None
        if isinstance(num_sampled, int) or step is None:
            return

        for metadata in step:
            postprocess_meta = metadata.commit_recoverssm_state(num_sampled)
            if postprocess_meta is None:
                continue
            assert state_indices is not None
            # RecoverSSM already restored the accepted state. Update its running
            # column and reset the next-step copy bias to the neutral value.
            _postprocess_recoverssm_align_kernel[(postprocess_meta.num_spec_decodes,)](
                idx_mapping,
                num_sampled,
                postprocess_meta.request_indices,
                postprocess_meta.num_computed_tokens,

                num_accepted_tokens,

            )

)

**LumoTree (arXiv:2609.23900v3, cs.LG, 04 Oct 2026; author Zhiyuan Ma)**

**Title history**
- The page shows only the v3 title: "LumoTree: Path-Parallel Speculative Verification for Hybrid Language Models."
- It does not mention any earlier title, so "GDN Tree-Scan" as a v1 title cannot be confirmed.
- The only version note concerns the artifact: version 1 predates the sampler correction and version 2 includes it (commit 9902ccca2).

**What it does**
- It performs tree speculative verification for recurrent-hybrid models, specifically Gated DeltaNet (GDN) combined with convolution and softmax attention.
- The tree is split into dependent path groups. Independent branch paths run in parallel, and each GPU program covers one path, head and value tile, reusing the state tile across the nodes in that path.
- "Boundary states connect dependent paths." The first path exports temporary cut states, and second-level branches start from them. The two levels run as separate GPU launches.
- **Commit is replay-based, not a fresh model forward.**
  - Verification records rounded per-node operands.
  - After acceptance, it replays "recorded operands through native GDN updates" from the pre-tree state, inside one captured committer graph with one native update per GDN layer.
  - The paper contrasts this with SpecLA, whose token-replay baseline regenerates factors. In LumoTree, cached operands are reused, but the recurrent updates along the accepted path are re-executed.
- The convolution history is gathered and the attention KV is remapped using the same logical-to-physical slot map. Physically, the principal spine is laid out first.
- Other parts of the serving cycle:
  - fused argmax/top-k draft selection;
  - device-resident acceptance;
  - CUDA graphs;
  - a patched FlashAttention-2 kernel with grouped query heads (pairs) and split-K 4.

**Serving engine**
- LumoTree is built on a forked vLLM; native MTP shares the same vLLM build.
- SGLang EAGLE (FlashInfer attention) is used only as a cross-stack comparison.
- llama.cpp is not mentioned.

# KVBuffer (arXiv:2605.19049v1): extraction

## (1) Speculative-decoding verification ("lazy commit")

"Lazy commit" is your term. The paper calls this parallel verification.

- **Mechanism:** The KVs of the draft tokens go into the buffer. Their outputs are computed in chunkwise form (Eq. 7: committed state S_{t−j} plus masked intra-chunk QKᵀV). The state is updated once, using only the accepted tokens (Eq. 8: S_t = S_{t−j} + K_accᵀV_acc).
- **No temporary states:** This replaces the recurrent approach. The paper says baselines must "compute a temporary linear attention state for each draft token and store these temporary states until draft tokens are verified."
- **GDN-specific buffer contents:** For each token it stores the decay factor α, the key k, and the delta value u. α is a scalar, so the extra storage is small.
- **Block size:** For speculative decoding, the KVBuffer block size equals the number of draft tokens.
- **Analytical speedup:** ((m+1)d + 2m)/(3d + 4m), which tends to (m+1)/3 when d ≫ m.
  - At m = 2 it roughly matches the recurrent form.
  - Above that, the speedup grows linearly with m.
  - This assumes the recurrent baseline is fused and reads the initial state only once.
- **Memory:** The authors estimate about m× more concurrent requests in the same memory budget.

## (2) Baseline SGLang cost (Qwen3-Next)

- **State slots:** The baseline keeps one state slot per request in a state pool. Speculative decoding consumes N extra slots, where N is the number of draft tokens.
- **State size:** The state is about 2MB per Gated DeltaNet layer, roughly 100× a per-token KV.
- **Extra memory:** "verifying 4 draft tokens occupies an additional 384MB of memory per-request."
- **Latency:** Recurrent verification latency grows linearly with the number of draft tokens.
- **Batch size:** The text gives no batch-size breakdown for verification latency. Batch-size results appear only for chunkwise decoding, where at batch size 1 chunkwise can be slower than recurrent because of kernel-launch overhead. The authors suggest CUDA Graphs to mitigate this.

## (3) Numbers

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Decoding latency reduction | up to 45.17%, buffer size 32 |
| Theoretical optimal buffer size | 2√d ≈ 22.63 (larger in practice due to GQA) |
| Head dimension d | 128 |
| Verification speedup, 8 draft tokens | 2.78× (predicted ≈3×) |
| 4 draft tokens | 5× max serving requests; up to 1.46× throughput |
| KV-only decoding | batch size 128; block size 16; faster when L < 128 |
| Hardware | 4× NVIDIA L40S, tensor parallel |
| Software | SGLang v0.5.10, Triton kernels |
| Precision | FP32 state, FP16 KV |
| Drafter / dataset | MTP draft model, ShareGPT |
| Model | Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct |

My inference, not stated in the paper: the 5× figure is consistent with 1 + 4 states per request being reduced to 1.

There is also a minor numbering inconsistency: the text cites Figure 4 for chunkwise results and Figure 6 for throughput, which doesn't match the captions.

## (4) Related work on speculative decoding

- **STree (Wu et al., 2025):** tree-based parallel verification for SSMs. The paper notes it "does not investigate the linear attention models" or the serving support needed for chunkwise computation.
- **General speculative decoding:** Leviathan et al. 2023 and EAGLE (Li et al. 2024).
- **Other hybrid-model serving work:** Marconi (prefix caching) and Prefill-as-a-Service.

## (5) ROCm/AMD

There are no statements about ROCm or AMD. The only hardware is NVIDIA, and the paper mentions CUDA Graphs. The kernels are written in Triton, but the paper makes no portability claim.

## (6) Venue

No venue is given. It is an arXiv preprint (cs.LG, v1, 18 May 2026) by Longwei Zou and Lin Zhong at Yale, supported in part by NSF Athena.

# Bole: tree speculative decoding for hybrid-attention models, extracted details

## (1) How existing systems verify trees on hybrid models, and what it costs

**How SGLang verifies (the paper's main baseline, v0.5.12)**
- It walks a T-node tree and applies the gated-delta recurrence one node at a time. That makes T sequential steps, even though every proposal token is known before the forward pass.
- It materializes a complete post-update GDN state for every node, because one in-place state cannot represent diverging branches. All rejected snapshots are then discarded.
- vLLM is only cited in general terms. The paper gives no vLLM measurements.
- Only tree verification is discussed. Chains get no separate treatment.

**Share of verification time spent in linear attention (Qwen3.5-9B, A100)**
- Growing the tree from 8 to 64 nodes raises linear-attention layers' share of the target forward from 4% to 27%.
- So linear attention does not dominate the whole forward pass.
- Within the serial verifier itself, state materialization takes 38% of time on A100 and 86% on GB10.

**Snapshot memory**
- Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 4×A100, T=32:
  - 36 GiB at B=8
  - 72 GiB at B=16
  - Bole's factors stay below 1 GiB in both cases.
- Table I, transient state per request:

| Model | Linear state | SGLang T=100 / T=200 | Bole T=100 / T=200 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4B / 9B | 48 MB | 4.7 / 9.4 GB | 57 / 113 MB |
| 27B | 144 MB | 14.1 / 28.1 GB | 151 / 302 MB |
| 122B-A10B | 144 MB | 14.1 / 28.1 GB | 142 / 283 MB |

  This works out to an 82–99× reduction.
- Table VI, non-cache speculation overhead (A100, B=4, 128 nodes, GiB):

| System | 4B | 9B | 27B | 122B |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SGLang-Tree | 8.72 | 8.74 | 24.00 | 28.04 |
| AdaServe | 7.79 | 7.81 | 21.00 | 25.04 |
| Bole | 1.53 | 1.55 | 2.42 | 6.52 |

**Per-layer GDN verify latency vs batch size (Table VII, Qwen3.5-9B, µs)**

| Platform | B | Serial | Bole | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A100 | 1 | 174 | 50.6 | 3.4× |
| A100 | 16 | 822 | 110 | 7.5× |
| GB10 | 1 | 333 | 66.6 | 5.0× |
| GB10 | 16 | 3420 | 443 | 7.7× |

- Achieved occupancy, serial → Bole: 1.9→15.0%, 11.4→41.4%, 6.6→43.1%, 16.4→58.9%.
- L1/shared throughput rises 1.8–4.1×.
- At B=16, Bole writes 9.8 MB per layer instead of 824 MB (84× less).

**When extra tokens stop being nearly free**
- The MLP GEMMs turn compute-bound at about 128 rows on A100 and about 256 rows on GB10.

## (2) Bole's method

**Closed form for parallel verification**
- The paper's equation: "O = D_P Q S_pre + C(I+G)^{-1} D_β(V − D_P K S_pre)".
- G uses ancestor-masked KKᵀ with decay ratios Pᵢ/Pⱼ and β. C uses ancestor-plus-self-masked QKᵀ.
- G is strictly lower triangular, and G^{d+1}=0, where d is the maximum depth.
- The inverse is therefore an exact finite Neumann sum of degree d. The paper states it is exact, not an approximation.

**Kernel (Triton)**
- A factor producer builds G and C once per layer and head into a scratch workspace, at O(T̃²d_k) cost.
- The value dimension is split into N_v = ⌈d_v/b_v⌉ tiles, one CTA each. Each CTA covers the whole tree.
- Each CTA runs d on-chip MMA rounds, Z ← −GZ, accumulating into U, then computes O = B₀ + CU.
- d_k is chunked by b_k with a single-stage pipeline.
- Working set is Θ(T̃² + T̃b_v + b_k(T̃+b_v)). The (b_k, b_v) pair comes from compile-time configurations.
- Only the O and U tiles are written to HBM.

**Pipeline**
- Topology (parent map, masks, depth) is built once per round and reused across layers.
- Stage 1: tree-parallel short convolution that follows parent links, fused with bias, SiLU and gates.
- Stage 2: factor construction (G, C).
- Stage 3: tiled solve and readout.

**Factorized state and commit**
- Bole keeps one immutable S_pre plus per-node factors P, K and U.
- Storage is Θ(Hd_kd_v) + Θ(TH(d_k+d_v+1)), instead of Θ(THd_kd_v).
- Commit: S_new = P_a·S_pre + (D_aK_a)ᵀU_a, computed as one batched matmul.
- One launch covers all linear layers and takes under 0.5% of forward latency.
- No rollback or copy-on-write is needed.

**Batch-wide verification budget**
- Cost model: T_ver = T_full(n, L) + T_linear(n, d) + T_dense(N) + T_other(N). Here n is node count, L is KV length, d is depth and N = Σnᵢ.
- Offline calibration, per configuration (model, GPU/parallelism, batch-size bucket, KV-length bucket, depth/template bucket):
  - Sweep N over the supported CUDA-graph capacities.
  - Take B_ver = the largest N with T_ver(N) ≤ (1+ε)·T_dec. The value of ε is not given.
- At runtime, existing batching metadata selects the configuration, and the stored capacity is looked up. The budget adapts by bucket lookup, not by online re-profiling.
- Allocation across requests:
  - Keep each tree's root.
  - Fill the rest with a global top-k over cumulative draft path probability ρ(v).
  - Because a child's probability cannot exceed its parent's, each request's selection stays prefix-connected.
  - Per-request budgets qᵢ come from a segmented count. Everything runs on the GPU inside the captured graph.
- Sensitivity (Qwen3.5-9B, MBPP, B=8): throughput peaks at 128 total tree tokens on A100 and 256 on GB10.

**Integration**
- About 6.2 kLoC of Python and Triton in SGLang.
- Trees are packed into a flat-ragged forest, with CUDA Graphs per capacity bucket.
- Sampling and commit run entirely on the GPU.

## (3) Setup and headline numbers

**Setup**
- Models: Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, 27B, and 122B-A10B (TP4, A100 only).
- Drafter: each model's native MTP head. Weights are unquantized.
- GPUs:
  - 4× A100 80GB SXM4 with NVLink (312 TFLOP/s, 2.04 TB/s).
  - DGX Spark GB10 (256 TFLOP/s, 128 GB LPDDR5x at 273 GB/s).
- Baselines: SGLang-AR, SGLang-Tree (native EAGLE-loop tree path), and AdaServe (ported into SGLang).
- STree is discussed only as related work, not as a baseline.
- Tree settings: top-k=4, depth ≤8, same total proposal budget for all tree methods.
- Batch sizes: 28 MBPP configurations; text references B=1, 4, 8 and 16.
- Datasets: MBPP, ShareGPT, GSM8K, CNN/DailyMail; online replay of Open-SWE-Traces (OpenHands).

**Throughput (MBPP)**
- Geometric mean: 2.74× over AR, 1.26× over the best speculative baseline.
- Peak speedups:

| Platform | vs AR | vs SGLang-Tree | vs AdaServe |
|---|---|---|---|
| A100 | 3.62× | 1.41× | 1.39× |
| GB10 | 4.72× | 2.03× | 2.06× |

- On GB10, the gain over the best baseline grows from 1.11–1.14× at B=1 to 1.70–2.03× at B=8.
- Only Bole runs 27B at B=8 without running out of memory; both speculative baselines OOM.

**Other workloads (B=4)**
- A100: 1.98–3.36× vs AR, 1.15–1.20× vs the faster speculative baseline.
- GB10: 2.85–4.12× vs AR, 1.38–1.45× vs the faster speculative baseline.
- Mean accepted tokens (MAT), Bole: 4.98 on CNN/DailyMail up to 7.08 on GSM8K.
- MAT on MBPP: about 6.4–6.9 for all systems, with Bole slightly highest.

**Online agent serving**

| Compared with | TTFT reduction | TPOT reduction |
|---|---|---|
| SGLang-AR | 15.8–64.3% | 37.6–67.6% |
| SGLang-Tree | 63.5–67.6% | 33.8–50.3% |
| AdaServe | 61.3–73.3% | 28.9–49.9% |

- These ranges don't fully match the abstract's "up to 67.6%/49.9%" vs the strongest tree baseline. Up to 73.3% (AdaServe) and 50.3% (SGLang-Tree) also appear.
- Prefix-cache hit rate (A100 / GB10):
  - Bole: 90.8% / 92.6%
  - SGLang-Tree: 69.7% / 58.3%
  - AdaServe: 69.3% / 59.8%
  - AR: 89.8% / 93.3%

**Ablation (cumulative, over SGLang-Tree, online workload)**
- Budget only: +5.3% on A100, +10.7% on GB10.
- Plus parallel solver: 1.21× on A100, 1.30× on GB10.
- Plus factorized state: 1.59× on A100, 2.23× on GB10.
- For 122B, transient state drops from 18.0 to 0.18 GiB.

## (4) Related work on SSM and linear-attention speculation

- **STree:** composes diagonal SSM transitions over trees. The paper says this "does not extend to the token-dependent, non-diagonal recurrence" of gated linear attention.
- **Hybrid serving:** Marconi (recurrent prefix caching), plus HLX and Pimba (Transformer–SSM hardware execution).
- **Models cited:** Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Linear, Qwen3.5.
- **General tree speculation:** Medusa, EAGLE-2/3, Sequoia, Yggdrasil, GTO, SpecInfer, DeFT, AdaServe.
- STree is the only SSM-specific speculative decoding work listed.

## (5) AMD/ROCm

There is no mention of AMD or ROCm. Only NVIDIA hardware (A100, GB10) and NVIDIA tools (nsys, ncu) are used. The kernels are written in Triton, but the paper makes no portability claim beyond porting to "other inference engines."

**Note:** the arXiv HTML carries an "HPCA 2027 Submission… Confidential Draft" header, although it is posted under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

## (1) How existing systems verify trees on hybrid models, and what it costs

**How SGLang verifies (the paper's main baseline, v0.5.12)**
- It walks a T-node tree and applies the gated-delta recurrence one node at a time. That makes T sequential steps, even though every proposal token is known before the forward pass.
- It materializes a complete post-update GDN state for every node, because one in-place state cannot represent diverging branches. All rejected snapshots are then discarded.
- vLLM is only cited in general terms. The paper gives no vLLM measurements.
- Only tree verification is discussed. Chains get no separate treatment.

**Share of verification time spent in linear attention (Qwen3.5-9B, A100)**
- Growing the tree from 8 to 64 nodes raises linear-attention layers' share of the target forward from 4% to 27%.
- So linear attention does not dominate the whole forward pass.
- Within the serial verifier itself, state materialization takes 38% of time on A100 and 86% on GB10.

**Snapshot memory**
- Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 4×A100, T=32:
  - 36 GiB at B=8
  - 72 GiB at B=16
  - Bole's factors stay below 1 GiB in both cases.
- Table I, transient state per request:

| Model | Linear state | SGLang T=100 / T=200 | Bole T=100 / T=200 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4B / 9B | 48 MB | 4.7 / 9.4 GB | 57 / 113 MB |
| 27B | 144 MB | 14.1 / 28.1 GB | 151 / 302 MB |
| 122B-A10B | 144 MB | 14.1 / 28.1 GB | 142 / 283 MB |

  This works out to an 82–99× reduction.
- Table VI, non-cache speculation overhead (A100, B=4, 128 nodes, GiB):

| System | 4B | 9B | 27B | 122B |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SGLang-Tree | 8.72 | 8.74 | 24.00 | 28.04 |
| AdaServe | 7.79 | 7.81 | 21.00 | 25.04 |
| Bole | 1.53 | 1.55 | 2.42 | 6.52 |

**Per-layer GDN verify latency vs batch size (Table VII, Qwen3.5-9B, µs)**

| Platform | B | Serial | Bole | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A100 | 1 | 174 | 50.6 | 3.4× |
| A100 | 16 | 822 | 110 | 7.5× |
| GB10 | 1 | 333 | 66.6 | 5.0× |
| GB10 | 16 | 3420 | 443 | 7.7× |

- Achieved occupancy, serial → Bole: 1.9→15.0%, 11.4→41.4%, 6.6→43.1%, 16.4→58.9%.
- L1/shared throughput rises 1.8–4.1×.
- At B=16, Bole writes 9.8 MB per layer instead of 824 MB (84× less).

**When extra tokens stop being nearly free**
- The MLP GEMMs turn compute-bound at about 128 rows on A100 and about 256 rows on GB10.

## (2) Bole's method

**Closed form for parallel verification**
- The paper's equation: "O = D_P Q S_pre + C(I+G)^{-1} D_β(V − D_P K S_pre)".
- G uses ancestor-masked KKᵀ with decay ratios Pᵢ/Pⱼ and β. C uses ancestor-plus-self-masked QKᵀ.
- G is strictly lower triangular, and G^{d+1}=0, where d is the maximum depth.
- The inverse is therefore an exact finite Neumann sum of degree d. The paper states it is exact, not an approximation.

**Kernel (Triton)**
- A factor producer builds G and C once per layer and head into a scratch workspace, at O(T̃²d_k) cost.
- The value dimension is split into N_v = ⌈d_v/b_v⌉ tiles, one CTA each. Each CTA covers the whole tree.
- Each CTA runs d on-chip MMA rounds, Z ← −GZ, accumulating into U, then computes O = B₀ + CU.
- d_k is chunked by b_k with a single-stage pipeline.
- Working set is Θ(T̃² + T̃b_v + b_k(T̃+b_v)). The (b_k, b_v) pair comes from compile-time configurations.
- Only the O and U tiles are written to HBM.

**Pipeline**
- Topology (parent map, masks, depth) is built once per round and reused across layers.
- Stage 1: tree-parallel short convolution that follows parent links, fused with bias, SiLU and gates.
- Stage 2: factor construction (G, C).
- Stage 3: tiled solve and readout.

**Factorized state and commit**
- Bole keeps one immutable S_pre plus per-node factors P, K and U.
- Storage is Θ(Hd_kd_v) + Θ(TH(d_k+d_v+1)), instead of Θ(THd_kd_v).
- Commit: S_new = P_a·S_pre + (D_aK_a)ᵀU_a, computed as one batched matmul.
- One launch covers all linear layers and takes under 0.5% of forward latency.
- No rollback or copy-on-write is needed.

**Batch-wide verification budget**
- Cost model: T_ver = T_full(n, L) + T_linear(n, d) + T_dense(N) + T_other(N). Here n is node count, L is KV length, d is depth and N = Σnᵢ.
- Offline calibration, per configuration (model, GPU/parallelism, batch-size bucket, KV-length bucket, depth/template bucket):
  - Sweep N over the supported CUDA-graph capacities.
  - Take B_ver = the largest N with T_ver(N) ≤ (1+ε)·T_dec. The value of ε is not given.
- At runtime, existing batching metadata selects the configuration, and the stored capacity is looked up. The budget adapts by bucket lookup, not by online re-profiling.
- Allocation across requests:
  - Keep each tree's root.
  - Fill the rest with a global top-k over cumulative draft path probability ρ(v).
  - Because a child's probability cannot exceed its parent's, each request's selection stays prefix-connected.
  - Per-request budgets qᵢ come from a segmented count. Everything runs on the GPU inside the captured graph.
- Sensitivity (Qwen3.5-9B, MBPP, B=8): throughput peaks at 128 total tree tokens on A100 and 256 on GB10.

**Integration**
- About 6.2 kLoC of Python and Triton in SGLang.
- Trees are packed into a flat-ragged forest, with CUDA Graphs per capacity bucket.
- Sampling and commit run entirely on the GPU.

## (3) Setup and headline numbers

**Setup**
- Models: Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, 27B, and 122B-A10B (TP4, A100 only).
- Drafter: each model's native MTP head. Weights are unquantized.
- GPUs:
  - 4× A100 80GB SXM4 with NVLink (312 TFLOP/s, 2.04 TB/s).
  - DGX Spark GB10 (256 TFLOP/s, 128 GB LPDDR5x at 273 GB/s).
- Baselines: SGLang-AR, SGLang-Tree (native EAGLE-loop tree path), and AdaServe (ported into SGLang).
- STree is discussed only as related work, not as a baseline.
- Tree settings: top-k=4, depth ≤8, same total proposal budget for all tree methods.
- Batch sizes: 28 MBPP configurations; text references B=1, 4, 8 and 16.
- Datasets: MBPP, ShareGPT, GSM8K, CNN/DailyMail; online replay of Open-SWE-Traces (OpenHands).

**Throughput (MBPP)**
- Geometric mean: 2.74× over AR, 1.26× over the best speculative baseline.
- Peak speedups:

| Platform | vs AR | vs SGLang-Tree | vs AdaServe |
|---|---|---|---|
| A100 | 3.62× | 1.41× | 1.39× |
| GB10 | 4.72× | 2.03× | 2.06× |

- On GB10, the gain over the best baseline grows from 1.11–1.14× at B=1 to 1.70–2.03× at B=8.
- Only Bole runs 27B at B=8 without running out of memory; both speculative baselines OOM.

**Other workloads (B=4)**
- A100: 1.98–3.36× vs AR, 1.15–1.20× vs the faster speculative baseline.
- GB10: 2.85–4.12× vs AR, 1.38–1.45× vs the faster speculative baseline.
- Mean accepted tokens (MAT), Bole: 4.98 on CNN/DailyMail up to 7.08 on GSM8K.
- MAT on MBPP: about 6.4–6.9 for all systems, with Bole slightly highest.

**Online agent serving**

| Compared with | TTFT reduction | TPOT reduction |
|---|---|---|
| SGLang-AR | 15.8–64.3% | 37.6–67.6% |
| SGLang-Tree | 63.5–67.6% | 33.8–50.3% |
| AdaServe | 61.3–73.3% | 28.9–49.9% |

- These ranges don't fully match the abstract's "up to 67.6%/49.9%" vs the strongest tree baseline. Up to 73.3% (AdaServe) and 50.3% (SGLang-Tree) also appear.
- Prefix-cache hit rate (A100 / GB10):
  - Bole: 90.8% / 92.6%
  - SGLang-Tree: 69.7% / 58.3%
  - AdaServe: 69.3% / 59.8%
  - AR: 89.8% / 93.3%

**Ablation (cumulative, over SGLang-Tree, online workload)**
- Budget only: +5.3% on A100, +10.7% on GB10.
- Plus parallel solver: 1.21× on A100, 1.30× on GB10.
- Plus factorized state: 1.59× on A100, 2.23× on GB10.
- For 122B, transient state drops from 18.0 to 0.18 GiB.

## (4) Related work on SSM and linear-attention speculation

- **STree:** composes diagonal SSM transitions over trees. The paper says this "does not extend to the token-dependent, non-diagonal recurrence" of gated linear attention.
- **Hybrid serving:** Marconi (recurrent prefix caching), plus HLX and Pimba (Transformer–SSM hardware execution).
- **Models cited:** Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Linear, Qwen3.5.
- **General tree speculation:** Medusa, EAGLE-2/3, Sequoia, Yggdrasil, GTO, SpecInfer, DeFT, AdaServe.
- STree is the only SSM-specific speculative decoding work listed.

## (5) AMD/ROCm

There is no mention of AMD or ROCm. Only NVIDIA hardware (A100, GB10) and NVIDIA tools (nsys, ncu) are used. The kernels are written in Triton, but the paper makes no portability claim beyond porting to "other inference engines."

**Note:** the arXiv HTML carries an "HPCA 2027 Submission… Confidential Draft" header, although it is posted under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

2606.01019v1 | 2026-05-31 | updated 2026-05-31
TITLE: Hybrid Verified Decoding: Learning to Allocate Verification in Speculative Decoding
AUTH: Xin Su, Dawid Majchrowski, Fangyuan Yu, Vanshil Atul Shah, Sebastian Rogawski, Pawel Morkisz, Anahita Bhiwandiwalla, Phillip Howard
ABS: Large Language Model (LLM) generation remains expensive because autoregressive decoding calls the model once for each new token. Speculative decoding reduces this cost by drafting multiple tokens and verifying them with the target model in one step, but its speedup depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. Parameter-free draft sources can propose long continuations at low cost in structured and agentic workloads, yet a cache match that looks promising at one generation step may have low payoff at the next. We propose Hybrid Verified Decoding, which predicts the accepted length of a cache draft before verification and uses this payoff estimate to choose between cache verification and a model-based drafter. Across three LLMs and sixteen datasets, Hybrid Verified Decoding is especially effective on agentic workflows, where it outperforms EAGLE3 in every setting with a 2.73x average speedup. Our analysis shows how prompt structure creates cache opportunities, how high-payoff cache drafts concentrate in a small part of the draft space, and how payoff-guided selection reduces sequential decoding work, pointing to runtime draft selection as a promising direction for speculative decoding.
====================================================================================================
2609.33051v2 | 2026-09-27 | updated 2026-10-06
TITLE: SketchSSM: Write to the Full State, Read from a Compact Sketch
AUTH: Omin Kwon, JoongWon Shin, Minseo Kim, Kurt Keutzer, Sehoon Kim, Jae W. Lee
ABS: Hybrid-attention models replace most softmax attention layers with linear attention, reducing KV-cache growth and enabling larger decode batches where recurrent-state access becomes a major bottleneck. ReplaySSM amortizes state updates by buffering keys and values, but each new query still requires a full-state read even though the state remains unchanged between state updates. We observe that low-rank state-weighted query approximation accurately preserves state-read outputs. Although future queries are unknown, the basis vectors used to approximate them can be fixed offline. Based on this observation, we introduce SketchSSM, which preserves full-state updates while approximating reads. At each state update, SketchSSM reads the full state once to precompute outputs for these basis vectors, storing them in a compact sketch. Each subsequent decode step combines the sketch vectors with query-dependent coefficients to reconstruct the output without a full-state read. Across four Mamba-2-, GDN-, and KDA-based models, SketchSSM at a mean sketch rank of 8 reduces state-access traffic by approximately 10$\times$ while matching the average accuracy of the FP32 full-state baseline across four decode benchmarks, and preserves recall on four RULER retrieval tasks. At this rank on one NVIDIA B300, linear-attention kernel speedups over the Standard vLLM baseline reach 7.30$\times$, 5.02$\times$, and 5.24$\times$ for Mamba-2, GDN, and KDA, respectively, with up to 2.77$\times$ higher decode throughput on Nemotron 3 Super.
====================================================================================================
2607.06763v2 | 2026-07-07 | updated 2026-07-12
TITLE: Trees from Marginals: Autoregressive drafting with factorized priors
AUTH: Yuma Oda, Ryan Mathieu, Roman Knyazhitskiy, Artur Chakhvadze
ABS: Speculative decoding greatly increases the interactivity of autoregressive language models by trading off computation for extra tokens generated in a single forward pass. Factorized draft models are especially efficient because they predict future-token marginals in parallel, but their independence assumption causes acceptance rates to degrade sharply as the speculative budget grows. We analyze this limitation and introduce Weaver, a lightweight autoregressive adapter that constructs proposal trees from the top-K marginals of a factorized drafter. Weaver restores conditional dependencies between proposed tokens while avoiding a full-vocabulary projection. To support fast verification for models with Gated Delta Net layers, we derive a rollback-free tree-verification algorithm and implement optimized CUDA kernels in SGLang. By combining these model and systems contributions we achieve a 4.37-fold speedup over autoregressive decoding, and outperform a highly optimized DFlash baseline by 24.7%.
====================================================================================================
2605.08301v1 | 2026-05-08 | updated 2026-05-08
TITLE: Priming: Hybrid State Space Models From Pre-trained Transformers
AUTH: Aditya Chattopadhyay, Elvis Nunez, Prannay Kaul, Benjamin Bowman, Evan Becker, Luca Zancato, David Thomas, Wei Xia ...
ABS: Hybrid State-Space models combine Attention with recurrent State-Space Model (SSM) layers, balancing eidetic memory from Attention with compressed fading memory from SSMs. This yields smaller Key-Value caches and faster decoding than Transformers, along with a richer architectural design space. Exploring that design space at scale has so far required training from scratch, a barrier that has kept most large-model Hybrid research within a narrow range of architectures. We introduce Priming, a method that turns Hybrid architecture design from a pre-training problem into a knowledge transfer one. Priming initializes a Hybrid model from a pre-trained Transformer and, through short alignment and post-training phases, recovers downstream quality using less than 0.5% of the source model's pre-training token budget. Priming is agnostic to the source Transformer family (e.g., Qwen, Llama, Mistral), model class (dense or Mixture-of-Experts), and model scale. Priming enables us to run the first controlled comparison of SSM layer types at scale under identical conditions. We evaluate, Gated KalmaNet (GKA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN), and Mamba-2, and show that their expressiveness hierarchy, GKA>GDN>Mamba-2, directly predicts downstream performance on long-context reasoning tasks. We scale Priming to 8B/32B reasoning models with native 128K contexts. Our Hybrid GKA 32B improves over its source Qwen3-32B by +3.8 average reasoning points, while staying within 1% of a Transformer post-trained on the same data and enabling up to 2.3x higher decode throughput. To foster research on Hybrid architectures, we release a model zoo of primed Hybrid models for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with the Priming training and inference code (Sequence Parallelism algorithms for long-context training, optimized GKA kernels, and vLLM serving plugin), all under Apache~2.0 License.

## The blog post: "Hybrid Models as First-Class Citizens in vLLM"
It was published on the PyTorch blog in November 2025. It was written by the vLLM team at IBM and explains how the vLLM community has elevated hybrid models from experimental hacks in V0 to first-class citizens in V1.

- **What hybrid models are:** Hybrid models like Qwen3-Next, Nemotron Nano 2, MiniMax-Text-01 and Granite 4.0 combine attention with alternatives such as Mamba or linear attention.
- **Memory comparison:** Attention layers rely on a paged KV cache, organized into 16-token blocks, each consuming about 64 KiB. For a 128k sequence, the KV cache can be nearly 200 times larger than the Mamba state.
- **The V0 problem:** KV cache was allocated efficiently as blocks, but the Mamba state was allocated separately. Each Mamba layer had a state tensor per active sequence, sized by the user-defined parameter max_num_seqs. Setting it too high risked CUDA out-of-memory errors, while setting it too low reduced concurrency.
- **Prefix caching:** It is now supported for hybrid models that use Mamba-2, although it is still experimental.
- **Benchmarks:** They were run on vLLM v0.10.2, the last release that supported hybrid models in both V0 and V1, so the two could be compared directly.
- **The new allocator:** vLLM solved this with its Hybrid Memory Allocator (HMA), rebuilt around a unified allocator.

## Mamba state per draft token in speculative decoding (from GitHub issues)
- **Separate state slots for draft tokens:** A bug report explains that some kernels "read and write only state slot 0 and never the k speculative slots. On a request's first decode step those slots have never been written; the next step's selective_state_update reads slot num_accepted - 1", which corrupts the recurrent state. The issue notes that a lower batch-reorder threshold only costs performance for normal token-KV attention, but "for backends with per-draft recurrent state it is a correctness bug." Suggested workaround: set "attention_backend": "TRITON_ATTN" in --speculative-config, or disable MTP.
- **Extra blocks for draft tokens:** In the Mamba backend's state index table, "The + num_speculative_blocks accounts for MTP draft tokens." One NemotronH bug report says turning on both Mamba prefix caching and MTP speculative decoding causes three cascading bugs during cudagraph profiling at startup.
- **Rolling back state:** On vllm-metal, using both together fails with this error: "draft-state rollback across mamba state blocks (num_speculative_blocks) is not implemented."
- **Disaggregated (P/D) deployments:** The vLLM Ascend docs say that for hybrid Mamba models (e.g., Qwen-Next and Qwen3.5 series), num_speculative_tokens should be equal on P nodes and D nodes.

## Related vLLM blog post
A later post explains how vLLM extends NIXL prefill/decode disaggregation to hybrid SSM-attention models, including Mamba conv-state transfer support. It describes Mamba state this way: there is no concept of "tokens" in these states; they are a fixed-size summary of the entire sequence history, so block_size for SSM is effectively 1.

I couldn't find one 2026 blog post that shows a hybrid Gated DeltaNet or Mamba model running slower with MTP than without it at high concurrency. Several recent sources do cover parts of that question, though.

**Why hybrid models make speculation harder**
- **TreeWY paper (arXiv, 2026):** Most layers in modern open models are Gated DeltaNet layers that keep a small, fixed-size recurrent state instead of a KV cache. This makes ordinary decoding memory-efficient, but hurts speculative decoding. To verify a batch of draft tokens and then roll back the rejected ones, today's systems snapshot the full recurrent state at every draft position for GDN layers. That makes wide draft trees too memory-hungry. The paper also mentions ReplaySSM, shipping concurrently July 2026 in a vLLM RFC and TensorRT-LLM, which saves the state much less often than every draft step.
- **PyTorch/SGLang blog (Dec 2025):** the in-place state updates preclude the ability to roll back cache entries for partial sequence matches, which complicates the implementation of many widely adopted features, such as prefix caching and speculative decoding.

**Concrete concurrency limit (SGLang Qwen3.8-Flash-Next guide, 4 days ago)**
This is the closest match to your query. The hybrid model reserves Mamba state slots for every running request. With the default settings, that allows 3 requests with MTP and 12 without on this card. After tuning, the measured numbers were 6.02 ms TPOT at 1 request with MTP, 675 output tok/s at 16; 906 output tok/s at 64 without. The ceilings are ~20 requests with MTP (each request carries 4 intermediate draft states) and ~70 without. So MTP lowers the maximum batch size, which caps total throughput.

**Throughput falling below no speculation**
- **vLLM issue #49548 (Qwen3.5-122B, a hybrid GDN model):** The dynamic speculation setting caused a catastrophic aggregate-throughput collapse under concurrency that looks like a pathological stall, not just "no speculation at high batch." Above the batch-size cutoff where speculation switches off, throughput was ~1.5–10× worse than a plain non-spec run would be.
- **Reducto Engineering (July 2026):** This post benchmarks MTP across concurrency levels to show when accepted speculative tokens improve throughput—and when verification overhead takes over. At low and moderate concurrency, verification is cheap enough for MTP to help. Its key point is that MTP does not have one concurrency threshold. Its benefits depend on request shape, output length, and how efficiently the target model verifies the resulting batch.
- **Lyceum (Sept 2026):** At high concurrency, continuous batching already maximizes GPU utilization. Speculative decoding then competes with real requests for compute, leading to a measured 1.8x slowdown on workloads like CNN DailyMail. It suggests testing with and without speculation at several concurrency levels, finding the point where the throughput curves cross, and turning speculation off above it.
- **vLLM blog on AMD GPUs (Aug 2026):** some settings produced smaller changes or throughput below the non-speculative baseline, while several model-workload combinations produced throughput ratios above 2×.

**Correctness bugs with Mamba + MTP under load**
- vLLM #55894: With MTP speculative decoding on a hybrid Mamba2 model (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16), some requests come back as garbled output. The suggested fix is to set "attention_backend": "TRITON_ATTN" (or any backend whose builder reports no threshold or 1 + k) in --speculative-config, or disable MTP.
- A Sept 25 digest of vLLM activity lists multiple reports of output degeneration and "Failed to advance FSM" errors under concurrency, specifically involving hybrid Mamba/Attention models (#56868, #49694, #55506).

**Workaround:** In vLLM, the --speculative-disable-by-batch-size 64 flag (vLLM) handles the automatic fallback for high-concurrency traffic. At batch sizes above 64, vLLM silently reverts to standard decoding. Issue #49548 suggests that a similar per-batch-size setting can stall on hybrid models, so benchmark it before relying on it.

I found several relevant results. The most direct match is a ROCm blog post about speculative decoding for Qwen3.5 on MI355X. Other sources cover native MTP, Gated DeltaNet kernels on AMD GPUs, and how to deploy with vLLM and SGLang.

**1. ROCm blog: DFlash vs. native MTP for Qwen3.5 on MI355X (about 3 weeks old)**
- AMD ran DFlash, a draft model that generates a block of tokens at once, on MI355X with vLLM and benchmarked it head-to-head against Qwen3.5's built-in MTP drafter, and then quantized the target model to mxfp4 to show that speculation and quantization stack.
- Results: DFlash delivers up to ~5× single-request throughput on Qwen3.5-27B (5.02× on MATH500) and up to 3.27× on the MoE 35B-A3B, beating native MTP on nearly every matched setting. On 27B HumanEval, DFlash reaches 10.38 accepted tokens per target step versus MTP's 8.02.
- Setup tip for the MoE model: the native fp4 MoE kernel must be enabled explicitly (VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1, AITER ≥ 0.1.16.post2); otherwise vLLM falls back to a dequant-to-bf16 path that cancels out the speedup.

**2. vLLM blog: speculative decoding on AMD GPUs (Aug 23, 2026)**
- The tests used selected Gemma, Qwen, MiniMax, and Kimi models on AMD Instinct™ MI300X and MI355X GPUs.
- This blog reached the opposite conclusion for some models: for Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and Qwen3.6-27B, the maximum measured native-MTP values within the tested sweeps were higher than the corresponding maximum DFlash values. The largest ratio in this group was 2.20× for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on MATH500. The two blogs used different setups, so their numbers aren't directly comparable.

**3. Gated DeltaNet kernels on ROCm**
- From AMD's Day 0 Qwen 3.5 post: The Gated Delta Networks in Qwen 3.5 are supported in vLLM via Triton-based kernels (fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule). Since SGLang and vLLM supports Triton on ROCm, these kernels work out-of-the-box on AMD GPU.
- vLLM PR #41446 aims to optimize GatedDeltaNet (Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5) FLA prefill kernels for AMD MI300X (gfx942). Validated end-to-end on Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8. It adds a fused kernel because on MI300X this exceeds the 256 MB Infinity Cache, so the round-trip dominates.

**4. SGLang on AMD**
- The SGLang Qwen3.5 cookbook says that on MI300X/MI325X/MI355X you should use SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 and SGLANG_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN=1 with --attention-backend aiter, which requires --page-size 16. It also suggests SGLANG_MAMBA_SSM_DTYPE=bfloat16 to store the Mamba SSM state in bfloat16.
- The current MI355X image is lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.20-rocm720-mi35x-20260927.

**5. Known issues and caveats**
- The vLLM recipe for Qwen3.5-397B, from February, said MTP-1 speculative decoding for AMD GPUs is under development. The later blogs above suggest this has improved since then.
- An open AITER issue (#6221), filed 18 hours ago, reports that MTP decode slows down as context grows on MI355X (gfx950) with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8. The cause is the default Gluon attention backend. By contrast, on gfx942 (MI325X) the Triton path runs in all of these configurations and nothing decays: MTP holds 160-185 t/s out to 30k.
- A third-party infrastructure digest from today mentions vLLM critical fixes for speculative decoding correctness and KV cache corruption in hybrid GDN + MTP configurations. It also warns that speculative decoding acceptance rates on ROCm may be badly degraded in current nightly builds.

I didn't find a ROCm blog post specifically about Qwen3-Next. The Qwen3-Next coverage I found is the vLLM GatedDeltaNet PR, which covers both Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5.

# Hybrid Models Meet SGLang: More than Full Attention

Source: https://pytorch.org/blog/hybrid-models-meet-sglang-more-than-full-attention/

Last updated: 2025-12-03

---

## Introduction

Hybrid models that combine the capabilities of full attention layers with alternatives—such as Mamba or linear attention—have gained more and more traction, especially in long-context large language model (LLM) serving scenarios. By leveraging linear attention, the KV cache memory consumption per request is bounded to a constant, and prefill latency can scale linearly with input length. This characteristic aligns well with real-world workloads, such as those in RAG queries, agentic tools, and thinking/reasoning patterns.

However, the in-place state updates preclude the ability to roll back cache entries for partial sequence matches, which complicates the implementation of many widely adopted features, such as prefix caching and speculative decoding. The request-level state storage required by Mamba states also imposes new challenges and demands on memory management and PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation.

This article discusses how SGLang has adapted to and optimized for the aforementioned challenges.

## What are State Space Models?

State space models (SSMs), and more generally linear RNNs and linear attention, such as Mamba, selectively compress tokens and context into a recurrent state. This recurrent state is of fixed size and is updated in place. By utilizing SSMs, memory consumption can be maintained at a constant level, and computational complexity scales linearly with sequence length, rather than quadratically. However, the purely linear structure is inherently limited by finite-state capacity, posing challenges for handling long-context or achieving strong recall capabilities.

To achieve a trade-off between efficiency and capacity, hybrid models have been proposed. These models interleave quadratic Attention layers with SSM layers at fixed intervals. As a result, hybrid models achieve strong performance across various tasks while preserving most of the efficiency advantages offered by SSM layers.

|  | Attention | SSM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Computational Complexity | O(N^2) | O(N) |
| Memory Consumption | O(N) | O(1) |

## Memory Management

### Design of Hybrid State Management  

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/hybrid.png)

In SGLang, hybrid linear models separate the memory pool into two parts: Mamba pool and KV cache pool. Both Mamba pool and KV cache pool memory sizes are fixed, hence the risk of CUDA out-of-memory errors is eliminated. Users can adjust the size ratio between Mamba pool and KV cache pool by changing server argument ***–mamba-full-memory-ratio*** according to workload. 

The main difference between Mamba pool and KV cache pool is that the former allocates Mamba state at the request level and the latter allocates at the token level. We use ***HybridReqToTokenPool*** to bind a Mamba state and a request so that the lifespan of requests and Mamba states are aligned. In addition, we use ***HybridLinearKVPool*** to map logical layer id to actual layer index in KV cache pool, so we do not need to allocate KV cache in linear layers, and memory size can be largely saved.

## Elastic Memory Pool

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2-2.png)

Hybrid models integrate diverse attention types, each maintaining its own memory pool with a dedicated allocator for GPU memory management. To maximize memory utilization and optimize inference performance, the ratios between memory pools must be configured according to workload characteristics. However, manually setting these ratios is nontrivial, and fluctuating workloads may render predefined ratios suboptimal during runtime. To address this, we propose an elastic memory pool that dynamically adjusts pool sizes under a fixed total GPU memory budget.

The elastic memory pool comprises resizable tensors and a centralized control module:

**Resizable Tensors via CUDA Virtual Memory Management**:

- A virtual address space is pre-allocated with oversubscribed capacity. A torch.Tensor is created within this space and reshaped to match the KV cache requirements.
- To expand a memory pool, physical CUDA memory pages are mapped to the appropriate virtual addresses, activating the corresponding KV cache blocks.
- To shrink a pool, idle KV cache blocks are disabled, and their physical pages are unmapped to free memory.

**Centralized Control Module:**

- During initialization, all memory pools register with the control module.
- At runtime, if a memory pool exhausts its capacity, it requests expansion. The control module identifies the most underutilized pool, issues a shrink command, and authorizes the requester to expand upon successful shrinkage.

With the Elastic Memory Pool in place, the system can dynamically adjust the allocation ratio between the Mamba pool and the KV Cache pool based on workload demands, maximizing GPU memory utilization to enable larger-batch inference.

## Optimizations and Adaptions

### Prefix Caching

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/3-2.png)

Prefix caching is a widely used optimization method in full attention models, which can save redundant computations across requests. However, the following properties about Mamba state make the prefix cache complicated: 1) SSM states are updated in-place, so a request’s states cannot be rolled back to represent its prefixes. 2) SSM states are orders of magnitude larger than the KVs of a single token. 3) Most of SSM states’ forward kernels exhibit “all or nothing” reusability.

SGLang supports prefix cache for hybrid linear models by implementing a hybrid radix tree named ***MambaRadixCache***. It mainly separates match / insert / evict parts:

- **match**: ***MambaRadixCache*** will return the best node where Mamba state value is not None and the key is the prefix of input. It needs to copy the Mamba state from the radix tree.
- **insert**: KV cache and Mamba states will be inserted into ***MambaRadixCache*** after chunked prefill or decoding stages. It needs to fork a checkpoint of Mamba state from a request.
- **evict**: ***MambaRadixCache*** keeps two LRU lists to maintain Mamba states and KV cache timestamps individually. KV cache must be evicted from leaves to root node and Mamba states can be evicted from any node.

By integrating ***MambaRadixCache***, hybrid linear models can use prefix caching without modifying linear attention kernels.

## Speculative Decoding

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/4-1.png)

For simplicity, we illustrate everything using the most basic linear-attention update,

  **Sₜ = Sₜ₋₁ + vₜ kₜᵀ**,

to keep the blog easy to follow. In real systems, the update is a bit more complex.

**Why does standard speculative decoding not work for SSMs?**

- SSM states update in-place, so rejected tokens cannot be rolled back.
- The [Eagle-Tree](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.15077) attention mask is incompatible with how SSM states are maintained.

**SGLang’s solution: one independent Mamba cache slot per draft token**

- Each draft token receives a private cache slot with its own SSM state

  - ***“the”*** → slot 1
  - ***“air”*** → slot 2
  - ***“streets”*** → slot 3
  - When a sequence of draft tokens is accepted, simply promote the last accepted slot to become the new main state.  

 (Example: after accepting ***“the streets are”***, slot 3 becomes the main SSM state.)

**EAGLE-Tree with Top-K > 1**

- Precompute parent indices before verification.

- For each drafted token:

  - Trace its parent using these indices.
  - Apply the recurrent update **S****new****= S****parent****+ v****new****k****new****ᵀ**

## Prefill and Decode disaggregation

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/5-1.png)

SGLang’s PD-disaggregation architecture supports hybrid models by extending the transfer protocol with a dedicated state transfer channel. Beyond standard paged KV cache transfers, the system transmits model-specific states (e.g., Mamba conv/temporal states, SWA sliding windows) through a parallel data path. 

**Mamba Integration Details: **

- Mamba models maintain two separate memory pools: a paged KV pool for full attention layers and a Mamba pool for linear layers storing conv and temporal states.
- When a new request arrives, it first undergoes prefix matching via the MambaRadixTree. If a cache hit occurs, the matched MambaState is copied into a new Mamba memory region to serve as the current request’s Mamba buffer, where the prefill inference continues to proceed. Upon prefill completion, the prefill instance transfers the final Mamba state as a single contiguous block to the decode instance, using the ‘dst_state_indices’ to identify the destination slot. Unlike paged KV transfers that can be streamed incrementally, Mamba states are transmitted atomically. 
- The decode instance pre-allocates both KV page slots and a dedicated Mamba slot, ensuring the received states are stored in the correct memory location for subsequent decode steps.

To integrate a new hybrid pool for disaggregated serving, only three steps are required upon current PD implementation: 

- expose state buffer pointers, sizes, and item lengths for transfer registration; 
- define state_indices preparation logic in both prefill and decode workers to specify which pool slots to transfer—this can be a single index per request (e.g., Mamba), page indices for windowed data (e.g., SWA), or full sequence indices (e.g., NSA); 
- register a unique state_type identifier in the KV manager and add corresponding transfer handling in the backend.

## Benchmark

Benchmarks were performed in SGLang v0.5.5, the latest released version. The server ran on H200 GPUs with ***Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8***.

### Prefix Caching

```
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 –tp 2
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang \
--dataset-name generated-shared-prefix \
--gsp-num-groups 50 \
--gsp-prompts-per-group 10 \
--gsp-system-prompt-len 10240 \
--gsp-question-len 256 \
--gsp-output-len 128 \
--max-concurrency 5  --port 30000
```

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/6-1.png)

## Speculative Decoding

python3 -m sglang.launch_server –model Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 –tp 2 –disable-radix-cache  –speculative-num-steps 2 –speculative-eagle-topk 1 –speculative-num-draft-tokens 3 –speculative-algo EAGLE

python3 -m sglang.test.send_one

![](https://pytorch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/7-1.png)

We tested ***Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8*** performance with **batch size = 1**.With a 2-token MTP window and topk=1, the system achieves a throughput of 257.20 tokens/sec, with an average acceptance length of 2.709 tokens.

With a 3-token MTP window and topk=1, throughput increases to 306.94 tokens/sec, with an average acceptance length of 3.413 tokens.

With a 4-token MTP window and topk=4 and draft tokens=8, throughput increases to 324.57 tokens/sec, with an average acceptance length of 4.231 tokens.

## Future Work

Feature work can be tracked [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/12867). More specifically, we plan to:

- More general prefix caching: including support page size > 1,  speculative decoding and other features. 
- Integrate into Hicache: fast hierarchical KV caching is an important feature for SGLang. We need to develop new query, storage and schedule mechanisms for KV cache in linear attention layers.
- Deterministic inference adaption: we hope to make adaptations for hybrid linear models to support bitwise training-inference consistency.

## Acknowledgement

SGLang Team: Yi Zhang, Biao He, Binyao Jiang, Ke Bao, Qingquan Song, Hanming Lu, Shangming Cai, Zhangheng Huang, Sicheng Pan, Baizhou Zhang
